chunks.title: Management of Malignant Pleural Effusions: An Official ATS/STS/STR Clinical Practice Guideline
chunks.content: Background: This guideline, a collaborative effort from the American Thoracic Society, Society of Thoracic Surgeons, and Society of Thoracic Radiology, aims to provide evidence-based recommendations to guide contemporary management of patients with a malignant pleural effusion (MPE). Methods: A multidisciplinary panel developed seven PICO questions and used GRADE and an Evidence-to-Decision framework. Results: The panel made conditional recommendations favoring ultrasound guidance for pleural interventions; avoiding pleural drainage in asymptomatic MPE; using either indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) or chemical pleurodesis in symptomatic patients with suspected expandable lung; performing large-volume thoracentesis to assess symptomatic response and lung expansion; using either talc poudrage or talc slurry for pleurodesis; using IPC over pleurodesis for nonexpandable lung, failed pleurodesis, or loculations; and treating IPC-associated infections with antibiotics without routine catheter removal. Conclusions: These recommendations can guide management of MPE to improve patient-centered outcomes.

chunks.title: Management of Malignant Pleural Effusions: An Official ATS/STS/STR Clinical Practice Guideline
chunks.content: Key evidence included observational comparative data showing reduced pneumothorax with ultrasound guidance during thoracentesis, retrospective cohorts suggesting asymptomatic small MPEs rarely require intervention, and randomized and nonrandomized comparative trials informing the choice between IPC and pleurodesis, as well as talc poudrage versus slurry in the context of expandable lung. For nonexpandable lung, evidence supported IPCs over pleurodesis. For IPC-associated infections, case series indicated most infections can be managed with antibiotics without catheter removal.

chunks.source_file: Management of significant airway bleeding during robotic assisted bronchoscopy a tailored approach.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Management of Significant Airway Bleeding during Robotic Assisted Bronchoscopy: A Tailored Approach
chunks.content: Robotic assisted bronchoscopy represents a major turning point in bronchoscopic history. The management strategies to address significant airway bleeding in this “robotic era” are not well documented, and further guidance is required. We present a case report that exemplifies our approach and management strategy using a combined and simultaneous flexible/robotic bronchoscopy if this complication is encountered.

chunks.source_file: Management of significant airway bleeding during robotic assisted bronchoscopy a tailored approach.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Management of Significant Airway Bleeding during Robotic Assisted Bronchoscopy: A Tailored Approach
chunks.content: Bleeding was noted traveling proximally along the robotic catheter and on fluoroscopy after needle sampling. Combined, simultaneous flexible/robotic bronchoscopy controlled the bleeding with ice cold saline and epinephrine. Hemostasis was confirmed bronchoscopically; clots were cleared; the robotic scope was reinserted and the procedure completed, including systematic mediastinal staging with EBUS. No pneumothorax, worsening hypoxemia, or other complications occurred. The patient was discharged home; pathology was nonmalignant; follow-up CT was planned in 3 months.

chunks.title: Guidelines for Management of Incidental Pulmonary Nodules Detected on CT Images: From the Fleischner Society 2017
chunks.content: The Fleischner Society updated its recommendations for the management of incidentally detected pulmonary nodules on CT in adults. The 2017 guidance raises the minimum threshold size for routine follow-up of solid nodules, provides ranges rather than fixed intervals for follow-up timing to allow individualized decision-making based on risk factors and patient preferences, combines solid and subsolid guidance into a single framework with specific advice for multiple nodules, and extends surveillance for subsolid nodules to 5 years. These consensus recommendations, informed by evidence from screening trials (NLST, NELSON, I-ELCAP, PanCan, BCCA) and expert opinion, aim to reduce unnecessary imaging while maintaining patient safety. The document also provides technical recommendations for CT acquisition (thin sections, low-dose protocols) and measurement practices.

chunks.title: Guidelines for Management of Incidental Pulmonary Nodules Detected on CT Images: From the Fleischner Society 2017
chunks.content: Key management recommendations: (1) Solid single nodules <6 mm: no routine follow-up in low-risk patients; optional 12-month CT in selected high-risk patients with suspicious morphology or upper lobe location. Solid 6-8 mm: CT at 6-12 months; consider 18-24 months (low risk) or perform CT at 6-12 months then 18-24 months (high risk). Solid >8 mm: consider CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling. (2) Multiple solid nodules: for <6 mm, no routine follow-up (low risk) or optional 12-month CT (high risk); for 6-8 mm and >8 mm, CT at 3-6 months then consider or perform CT at 18-24 months; manage by the most suspicious nodule. (3) Single subsolid nodules: pure ground-glass ≥6 mm: CT at 6-12 months to confirm persistence, then every 2 years until 5 years; part-solid ≥6 mm: CT at 3-6 months to confirm persistence; if unchanged and solid component remains <6 mm, annual CT for 5 years; persistent part-solid nodules with solid component ≥6 mm are highly suspicious. Subsolid <6 mm: generally no routine follow-up; consider follow-up at 2 and 4 years for selected suspicious ground-glass nodules. (4) Multiple subsolid nodules: CT at 3-6 months; if stable, consider CT at 2 and 4 years; subsequent management guided by the most suspicious nodule(s); multiple <6 mm pure ground-glass nodules are usually benign, but consider follow-up in selected high-risk patients at 2 and 4 years. General technical recommendations include use of thin-section reconstructions ≤1.5 mm, low-dose follow-up CT with CTDIvol ≤3 mGy in a standard-size patient, and consistent acquisition/reconstruction parameters. Prior imaging should be reviewed to assess stability. Measurements should use the average of long and short axes on the plane showing the greatest dimensions, rounded to the nearest millimeter; volumetry may be used with consistent software.

chunks.source_file: Mechanical properties of different airway sten.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Mechanical properties of different airway stents
chunks.content: Airway stents improve pulmonary function and quality of life in patients suffering from airway obstruction. The aim of this study was to compare main types of stents (silicone, balloon-dilated metal, self-expanding metal, and covered self-expanding metal) in terms of their mechanical properties and the radial forces they exert on the trachea. Mechanical measurements were carried out using a force gauge and specially designed adaptors fabricated in our lab. Numerical simulations were performed for eight different stent geometries, inserted into trachea models. The results show a clear correlation between stent diameter (oversizing) and the levels of stress it exerts on the trachea. Compared with uncovered metal stents, metal stents that are covered with less stiff material exert significantly less stress on the trachea while still maintaining strong contact with it. The use of such stents may reduce formation of mucosa necrosis and fistulas while still preventing stent migration. Silicone stents produce the lowest levels of stress, which may be due to weak contact between the stent and the trachea and can explain their propensity for migration. Unexpectedly, stents made of the same materials exerted different stresses due to differences in their structure. Stenosis significantly increases stress levels in all stents.

chunks.source_file: Mechanical properties of different airway sten.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Mechanical properties of different airway stents
chunks.content: Validation: Simulated smooth silicone stent stress-strain closely matched measurements (max strain 0.175 vs 0.2; elastic modulus ~1 MPa simulation vs 0.3 MPa measured). Bench testing: Covered metal stents were stiffer than uncovered; internally-covered metal stent (A) had higher yield stress than externally-covered (B): 15.7 kPa vs 12.3 kPa. Silicone stent exhibited a narrow linear region and higher stiffness within that region; shape distortion occurred at higher loads. Simulations: Stent diameter strongly increased stress. Example for a metal stent in healthy trachea: ~50 MPa (14 mm), ~100 MPa (15 mm), ~150 MPa (16 mm). With 30% stenosis, maximum stress rose markedly to ~400 MPa (14 mm), ~700 MPa (15 mm), and ~1000 MPa (16 mm), with non-symmetric stenosis typically highest. Material effects: stiffer metals (cobalt alloys, stainless steel 316L; E ≈ 190 GPa) generated higher stresses than nitinol (E ≈ 83 GPa). Covered metal stents exerted lower stresses than uncovered while maintaining contact. Silicone (both smooth and studded) exerted the lowest stresses; higher-stiffness silicone produced higher stresses than lower-stiffness silicone. Structural geometry notably influenced stress, even with identical materials.

chunks.source_file: Metallic Endobronchial Stents A Contemporary R.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Metallic Endobronchial Stents: A Contemporary Resurrection
chunks.content: Airway stenting has been practiced for several decades. It is one of the most common procedures performed by interventional pulmonologists. Typically, these stents are implanted to maintain the tubular patency of the tracheobronchial tree. They are only considered as a temporizing measure, or when a surgical option cannot be pursued. Through the past several decades, a number of metallic airway stents have been introduced into the market. First generation stents were comparatively simplistic and crafted from stainless steel. The latest generation of metallic airway stents are hybrid in nature and constructed with complex alloys. As airway stenting become more widely practiced, concerns arose regarding their safety. However, with improved understanding of stent-airway interactions, advancements in biomedical engineering, and a larger emphasis on post procedural care, the use of metallic endobronchial stents has been resurrected. We present the history, technological advancement, and contemporary indications of metallic airway stents.

chunks.source_file: Metallic Endobronchial Stents A Contemporary R.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Metallic Endobronchial Stents: A Contemporary Resurrection
chunks.content: Early generation metallic airway stents (Gianturco Z-stent, Wallstent) were associated with substantial late complications (migration, granulation, secretions retention), including one reported fatality in an early series of 55 patients. Second-generation devices (Palmaz, Strecker, AERO, Ultraflex, Dynamic Y) and third-generation nitinol-based hybrid stents (Bonastent, Silmet, Hanarostent, Carina-Y) showed improved deliverability and safety profiles in small series, though migration, mucus retention, and tissue overgrowth remain concerns. In a 12-patient Palmaz series, technical success was 100% with 10 patients improving clinically and 5 deaths reported (unrelated to the stent). In a 3-patient AERO series (6 stents), 5/6 stents migrated and all 6/6 stents developed thick mucus buildup; strictures recurred in all 3/3 patients. For the Dynamic Y stent, among 135 patients followed 3 months, 2 deaths due to hemoptysis and 4 migrations were reported. For Silmet, in 52 patients, technical success occurred in 51/52 and radiographic improvement in 25/52; tumor overgrowth and migration were reported as percentages without exact counts.

chunks.source_file: Moderate sedation changes for bronchoscopy in 2017.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Moderate Sedation Changes for Bronchoscopy in 2017
chunks.content: The reimbursement for procedures using moderate (conscious) sedation changed significantly as of January 1, 2017. Due to increasing use of anesthesia services to provide moderate sedation during endoscopy, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) removed work relative value units from many services requiring moderate sedation, including bronchoscopy codes. If a bronchoscopist provides moderate sedation without anesthesia services or another qualified provider, that work and revenue can be reclaimed by using the relevant CPT codes. Understanding the recent coding and billing changes is essential for appropriate reimbursement.

chunks.source_file: Moderate sedation changes for bronchoscopy in 2017.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Moderate Sedation Changes for Bronchoscopy in 2017
chunks.content: CMS removed 0.25 work RVU from many bronchoscopy CPT codes effective January 1, 2017, to account for bundled moderate sedation work. New CPT/HCPCS moderate sedation codes 99151-99157 allow separate reporting when appropriate. For patient age ≥ 5 years, same-physician sedation uses 99152 for the initial 15 minutes and 99153 for each additional 15 minutes; when provided by a second qualified provider in a facility, use 99156 then 99157. Initial codes should not be reported if sedation time is < 10 minutes. In facility settings, 99153 has no physician work RVU and is paid as practice expense to the facility. If a second provider performs moderate sedation, there is an approximate national average reimbursement decrease of 8.72 per procedure for the bronchoscopist.

chunks.title: Multidetector CT Evaluation of Tracheobronchomalacia
chunks.content: Tracheobronchomalacia is caused by weakness of tracheobronchial walls and supporting cartilage leading to excessive expiratory airway collapse. Because routine end-inspiratory chest radiographs and CT are often nondiagnostic, dynamic maneuvers such as forced exhalation or coughing are needed for detection. Advances in multidetector CT enable noninvasive diagnosis with accuracy comparable to bronchoscopy. This review details clinical indications, physiologic principles, diagnostic criteria, MDCT protocols including dynamic expiration and cine coughing techniques, reconstruction methods, image interpretation pearls, radiation dose management, and pre- and postoperative assessment considerations.

chunks.title: Multidetector CT Evaluation of Tracheobronchomalacia
chunks.content: Greater than 50 percent expiratory reduction in cross-sectional airway area is widely used as a diagnostic threshold for tracheomalacia, but healthy individuals may exceed this at end-expiration. In one cited study, 4 of 10 healthy young adult male volunteers had greater than 50 percent collapse at end-expiration on electron-beam CT, supporting a more conservative threshold of 70 percent in some contexts, especially during robust maneuvers like coughing on 64-MDCT. Dose-length product is approximately 500 mGy·cm for a dual-phase study with standard-dose inspiratory and low-dose dynamic-expiratory sequences in a 70 kg adult, approximately 200 to 220 mGy·cm for a single low-dose cine acquisition, and approximately 600 mGy·cm is a reference value for routine chest CT. Low-dose dynamic expiratory imaging at approximately 40 to 80 mA showed no degradation in tracheal lumen assessment compared with standard current in a clinical study. Image interpretation emphasizes paired inspiratory-expiratory comparisons, quantitative cross-sectional area measurements at matched levels, recognition of the expiratory 'frown sign' with membranous wall bowing, and use of sagittal MPRs to map craniocaudal extent.

chunks.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines): Lung Cancer Screening, Version 2.2024 — October 18, 2023
chunks.content: The NCCN Lung Cancer Screening Guidelines (Version 2.2024) provide consensus-based recommendations for identifying high-risk individuals and managing findings from low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening. The panel recommends annual LDCT for adults at high risk (age ≥50 years and ≥20 pack-year cigarette smoking history) with shared decision-making and access to curative-intent treatment. The document details nodule management based on nodule type (solid, part-solid, nonsolid), incorporates Lung-RADS for reporting, and outlines updates including imaging terminology (FDG-PET/CT), slice width preferences, and follow-up intervals for nonsolid nodules.

chunks.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines): Lung Cancer Screening, Version 2.2024 — October 18, 2023
chunks.content: Key updates from Version 2.2023 to Version 1.2024 and retained in Version 2.2024 include: revision of PET/CT terminology to FDG-PET/CT; reinforced multidisciplinary management; emphasis on radon and occupational exposures in risk discussions; encouragement to use risk calculators; expanded clarification that curative-intent options include surgery, SBRT/SABR, and ablation; acknowledgment of higher lung cancer risk among Black/African American individuals at lower smoking exposures; refined nodule definitions and measurement on lung windows; management pathways updated for solid nodules ≥15 mm including CT with contrast and/or FDG-PET/CT and/or tissue sampling; addition of pathways after bronchoscopy to either continue annual LDCT if no cancer or follow NSCLC guidelines if cancer confirmed; slice width preference revised to ≤2.5 mm with ≤1.5 mm preferred; nonsolid nodules require thin-slice review to exclude solid components; for nonsolid nodules, NCCN did not harmonize with Lung-RADS 1.1’s <30 mm annual threshold and instead recommends earlier 6-month evaluation for baseline or new nonsolid nodules ≥20 mm; and a new note emphasizing incorporation of patient preferences when deciding between 6-month LDCT follow-up and invasive procedures.

chunks.title: Nd-YAG Laser vs Bronchoscopic Electrocautery for Palliation of Symptomatic Airway Obstruction: A Cost-Effectiveness Study
chunks.content: Study objective: To evaluate the cost effectiveness of the Nd-YAG laser and bronchoscopic electrocautery for palliation in patients with symptomatic tumor obstruction. Design: A retrospective study. Setting: Bronchoscopy unit of a university hospital. Patients and intervention: Thirty-one consecutive patients with inoperable non-small cell lung cancer and symptomatic intraluminal tumor underwent bronchoscopic treatment. Dyspnea relief was the primary goal of treatment. Fourteen patients were treated with the Nd-YAG laser and 17 patients with electrocautery. Measurements and results: Improvement of symptoms was achieved in 70% of patients treated by either Nd-YAG laser or electrocautery. Mean ± SD survival was 8.0 ± 2.5 months after Nd-YAG laser treatment and 11.5 ± 3.5 months after electrocautery. The number of treatment sessions per patient was comparable: Nd-YAG laser, 1.1; electrocautery, 1.2. Duration of hospital stay was longer in patients treated with the Nd-YAG laser (8.4 vs 6.7 days). Average treatment costs, including admission charges, were $5,321 to $5,324 for the Nd-YAG laser and $4,290 for electrocautery. Higher costs in the group treated with the Nd-YAG laser were caused by a longer hospital stay before bronchoscopic treatment. Costs of equipment (electrocautery $6,701 and Nd-YAG laser $208,333), write-offs, maintenance, and repair were not included.

chunks.title: Nd-YAG Laser vs Bronchoscopic Electrocautery for Palliation of Symptomatic Airway Obstruction: A Cost-Effectiveness Study
chunks.content: Thirty-one patients were included: 14 treated with Nd-YAG laser and 17 with electrocautery. Groups were comparable in demographics, diagnosis, site of obstruction, timing, and antitumor therapy. General anesthesia was more common with Nd-YAG. Symptom improvement occurred in about 70% in both groups (Nd-YAG 10/14; electrocautery 13/17). No complications directly attributable to technique were reported; single events included hypotension (Nd-YAG) and hemoptysis/respiratory failure (electrocautery). Mean survival after treatment was 8.0 ± 2.5 months (Nd-YAG) vs 11.5 ± 3.5 months (electrocautery). Sessions per patient were similar (1.1 vs 1.2). Hospital stay before intervention was longer for Nd-YAG (8.4 ± 4.0 vs 6.7 ± 5.3 days) and after intervention similar (3.3 ± 2.5 vs 1.7 ± 1.6 days). Average total costs per patient within 1 month were higher with Nd-YAG ($5,324) vs electrocautery ($4,290); equipment costs were not included. Differences were mainly due to longer pre-intervention hospital stay with Nd-YAG.

chunks.title: Nd:YAG Laser Therapy in Lung Cancer: An 11-Year Experience with 2,253 Applications in 1,585 Patients
chunks.content: Between April 1982 and March 1993, 1,585 patients with significant symptoms of malignant airway obstruction were treated with 2,253 tracheobronchial neodymium (Nd):YAG laser resections performed by the first author only: 1,274 patients had non-small cell lung cancers, 91 small cell lung cancers, 105 metastatic tumors, 61 rare malignant tumors, and 81 unclassifiable carcinomas. More than 90% of the Nd:YAG laser resections were performed with rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia (sedation plus analgesia with spontaneous ventilation). Almost all the cases (93%) showed immediate good results based on clinical, radiological, and endoscopic follow-up. Rapid regrowth of tumor is the major limitation; in our series the median time between the first and the second treatment was 100 days. Complications have been few to date: 18 hemorrhages, 6 pneumothoraxes, and 10 deaths. The mortality rate was 0.44%. Although laser resection is a palliative treatment, since 1983 we have treated 19 carcinomas in situ and none has recurred. This is also the case for some early endoluminal metastases. Finally, 17 patients with bronchogenic carcinoma that seemed inoperable did have surgery after laser therapy and another 21 underwent less extensive surgery than initially planned. Nd:YAG laser photoresection, in experienced hands, can be used safely and successfully to open airways obstructed by tumor growth while controlling bleeding. Its primary use is in the trachea and in the main bronchi.

chunks.title: Nd:YAG Laser Therapy in Lung Cancer: An 11-Year Experience with 2,253 Applications in 1,585 Patients
chunks.content: From April 1982 to March 1993, 1,884 tracheobronchial tumors were treated by Nd:YAG laser, including 1,585 lung cancer patients (2,253 treatments), 143 tumors with uncertain prognosis, and 156 benign tumors. Among 1,419 bronchogenic carcinomas, immediate results were very good in 1,314 (93%) and unsatisfactory in 105 (7%), with results depending more on location and macroscopic appearance than histology. The median interval between the first and second treatment was 100 days (vs 29 days for a prior cohort treated with mechanical resection alone). Nineteen carcinomas in situ were treated with curative intent since 1983 and none recurred. Seventeen patients initially deemed inoperable underwent surgery after laser therapy, and 21 underwent less extensive surgery than initially planned. Complications among 2,253 malignant resections included hemorrhage >250 ml in 18, transient pneumothorax in 6, and 10 deaths (mortality 0.44%). Additional reported serious peri-procedural events: respiratory failure 12 (3 deaths), cardiac arrest 10 (4 deaths), myocardial infarction 4 (2 deaths), and pulmonary embolism 1 (1 death).

chunks.source_file: Novel bronchoscopic management of airway bleeding with absorbable gelatin and thrombin slurry.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Novel Bronchoscopic Management of Airway Bleeding With Absorbable Gelatin and Thrombin Slurry
chunks.content: Background—Airway bleeding, either spontaneous or as a result of bronchoscopy, is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Multiple bronchoscopic techniques are available to achieve complete hemostasis or as a bridge to definitive therapies. Methods—We report our experience on the feasibility of endobronchial instillation of an absorbable gelatin and thrombin slurry (GTS) for the treatment of spontaneous hemoptysis and procedure-related bleeding. Results—We identified thirteen cases in which GTS was used for endobronchial hemostasis when standard bronchoscopic measures like cold saline, epinephrine and in some cases balloon occlusion were not successful. GTS was delivered through the working channel of the bronchoscope in ten cases and through the distal port of a bronchial blocker in the remaining three. Median age was 69 years (range 52 to 79 years). Eight cases corresponded to spontaneous hemoptysis and five cases to diagnostic or therapeutic procedures. Bleeding was considered severe in nine (70%) cases. All but one case were associated with malignancy. Hemostasis was achieved in ten (77%) cases by using standard measures in addition to GTS. No patient adverse events at 30 days or damage to the equipment were identified. Conclusion—Bronchoscopic instillation of an absorbable gelatin and thrombin slurry is feasible and may be used in cases of spontaneous or procedure-related bleeding in addition to conventional measures. It can be delivered through the working channel of the bronchoscope or through the distal port available in some bronchial blockers. Controlled studies are necessary to determine the safety and efficacy of this novel technique.

chunks.source_file: Novel bronchoscopic management of airway bleeding with absorbable gelatin and thrombin slurry.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Novel Bronchoscopic Management of Airway Bleeding With Absorbable Gelatin and Thrombin Slurry
chunks.content: Thirteen uses of GTS (June 2010 to April 2017) were identified; one patient received GTS on two separate occasions. Median age was 69 years (range 52-79); six female and seven male. Eight cases had spontaneous bleeding (one surgical stump, others malignant airway disease); five were procedure-related (tumor debulking, transbronchial lung biopsy, or contact with endobronchial mass). Bleeding severity: severe in nine (70%), moderate in two (15%), mild in two (15%). No patient was on therapeutic anticoagulation and no significant coagulopathy was recorded. GTS was delivered via a bronchial blocker distal port in three cases; via bronchoscope working channel in ten cases; four of these had concomitant Fogarty balloon occlusion. Hemostasis was achieved bronchoscopically in ten cases (77%); two had a preemptive bronchial blocker left deflated. Additional measures included epinephrine in eleven cases (84%), and tamponade with embolectomy balloon and/or bronchial blocker in nine cases (70%). Two cases used oxidized cellulose polymer; two used more than one Gelfoam Plus kit. Recurrence of bleeding occurred in five of ten cases (50%) with initial hemostasis; only one required an additional therapeutic bronchoscopy. Failure to achieve hemostasis occurred in three cases (23%): all required post-bronchoscopy bronchial balloon occlusion; two required embolization; one resolved spontaneously. No patients required surgery. Three patients died within 30 days (two in the hemostasis group, one in the failure group with evident recurrent contributory bleeding); all deaths related to underlying malignancy. No complications attributable to GTS were identified at 30 days (no post-obstructive pneumonia, respiratory failure due to obstruction, dislodgement of GTS clot, or removal difficulty). No damage to bronchoscopy equipment was encountered.

chunks.source_file: Novel bronchoscopic management of airway bleeding with absorbable gelatin and thrombin slurry.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Novel Bronchoscopic Management of Airway Bleeding With Absorbable Gelatin and Thrombin Slurry
chunks.content: Bleeding rate: 50.0%

chunks.source_file: Occupational adverse effects and protective factors in bronchoscopy .oe_final.json
chunks.title: Occupational adverse effects and protective factors in bronchoscopy
chunks.content: The application of bronchoscopy has resolved a series of diagnostic and treatment challenges in pulmonary diseases. However, the occupational adverse effects experienced by healthcare workers in interventional pulmonology should receive increasing attention. Various aspects of adverse effects in bronchoscopy are often neglected, and healthcare workers frequently ignore guidelines for personal protection against factors such as radiation, smoke, pathogenic microbiological aerosols, cryogenic gas, etc. Thus, there is an urgent need to conduct additional research to establish standards for occupational adverse effects and protective measures related to bronchoscopy.

chunks.source_file: Occupational adverse effects and protective factors in bronchoscopy .oe_final.json
chunks.title: Occupational adverse effects and protective factors in bronchoscopy
chunks.content: Key findings summarized: (1) Occupational radiation exposure in bronchoscopy is generally low per procedure but cumulative exposure warrants adherence to protection principles (time, distance, shielding). Reported operator doses include median 0.4 µSv per EBUS with fluoroscopy and 12 µSv for EBUS-GS with 7.6 min fluoroscopy; CT fluoroscopy increases operator dose relative to conventional CT. ICRP recommends ≤20 mSv/year occupational limit. (2) Radioactive particle implantation with 125I shows surface dose attenuation over distance and time, approaching background at 50 cm and by 6 months; protective measures and post-operative precautions outlined. (3) Surgical smoke from laser/electrocautery/argon plasma contains ultrafine particles, chemicals (e.g., CO, acrylonitrile, benzene), viable pathogens/viruses, and possibly cancer cells; NIOSH recommends smoke evacuators with 31-46 m/s capture velocity and placement within 5 cm of the source; high-filtration masks and eye/skin protection are advised. (4) Lasers pose eye/skin beam hazards; protective eyewear and controls are required.

chunks.title: Operating Room Fires
chunks.content: Operating room fires are rare but devastating events. Guidelines are available for the prevention and management of surgical fires; however, these recommendations are based on expert opinion and case series. The three components of an operating room fire are present in virtually all surgical procedures: an oxidizer (oxygen, nitrous oxide), an ignition source (i.e., laser, “Bovie”), and a fuel. This review analyzes each fire ingredient to determine the optimal clinical strategy to reduce the risk of fire. Surgical checklists, team training, and the specific management of an operating room fire are also reviewed.

chunks.title: Operating Room Fires
chunks.content: Key quantitative findings summarized in the review include: (1) Operating room fires occur at least 650 times annually, with 2-3 patient deaths per year; most occur in the head/neck/upper chest (85%) and during monitored anesthesia care (81%). (2) Local oxygen concentration can exceed 35-50% under surgical drapes with open oxygen delivery at 6 L/min; nasal cannula flows can produce up to 60-70% local oxygen concentrations at higher flow rates. (3) In a benchtop experiment comparing skin preps, alcohol-based prep ignited in 13/60 samples with no drying versus 0/40 with non-alcohol-based prep (p<0.001), and 6/60 versus 0/40 after 3 minutes of drying (p=0.08), using a 2-second activation of a monopolar electrosurgical pencil. (4) Lasers can ignite endotracheal tubes in under 2 seconds in 100% oxygen. (5) Closed systems and mitigation strategies (e.g., FiO2 ≤30% with open delivery, open draping, suctioning under drapes, CO2 flooding, saline-soaked gauze) reduce fire risk.

chunks.title: Quality-Adjusted Survival Following Treatment of Malignant Pleural Effusions With Indwelling Pleural Catheters
chunks.content: Background: Malignant pleural effusions (MPEs) are a frequent cause of dyspnea in patients with cancer. Although indwelling pleural catheters (IPCs) have been used since 1997, there are no studies of quality-adjusted survival following IPC placement. Methods: With a standardized algorithm, this prospective observational cohort study of patients with MPE treated with IPCs assessed global health-related quality of life using the SF-6D to calculate utilities. Quality-adjusted life days (QALDs) were calculated by integrating utilities over time. Results: A total of 266 patients were enrolled. Median quality-adjusted survival was 95.1 QALDs. Dyspnea improved significantly following IPC placement (P < .001), but utility increased only modestly. Patients who had chemotherapy or radiation after IPC placement (P < .001) and those who were more short of breath at baseline (P = .005) had greater improvements in utility. In a competing risk model, the 1-year cumulative incidence of events was death with IPC in place, 35.7%; IPC removal due to decreased drainage, 51.9%; and IPC removal due to complications, 7.3%. Recurrent MPE requiring repeat intervention occurred in 14% of patients whose IPC was removed. Recurrence was more common when IPC removal was due to complications (P = .04) or malfunction (P < .001) rather than to decreased drainage. Conclusions: IPC placement has significant beneficial effects in selected patient populations. The determinants of quality-adjusted survival in patients with MPE are complex. Although dyspnea is one of them, receiving treatment after IPC placement is also important. Future research should use patient-centered outcomes in addition to time-to-event analysis. Trial registry: ClinicalTrials.gov; No.: NCT01117740.

chunks.title: Quality-Adjusted Survival Following Treatment of Malignant Pleural Effusions With Indwelling Pleural Catheters
chunks.content: 266 patients enrolled (196 pathology-proven MPE; 70 clinical diagnosis). Median QALDs 95.1 (95% CI 73.3-116.5). Utility did not significantly improve at 1 month vs baseline (difference 0.023; 95% CI -0.004 to 0.05; P = .10). Dyspnea improved substantially (Borg difference -2.31; 95% CI -2.66 to -1.95; P < .0001). Greater utility improvements were seen in those receiving chemotherapy/radiation after IPC (P < .001) and with higher baseline Borg (P = .005). Overall survival: 156/266 died; median 171 days (95% CI 130-192). Quality of life and lower dyspnea burden associated with longer survival; per 0.1 utility increase, death risk decreased by 36% (P < .001). Complications occurred in 26/266 patients (31 events total); 15/266 (5.6%) required IPC removal. Median time to any complication 1.4 months. IPC removal occurred in 148/266 (55.6%): decreased drainage 127, complication 15, other 6. Among those removed, recurrent effusion requiring intervention occurred in 21/148 (14%); median time to recurrence 3.8 months. Competing risks at 1 year: death without removal 35.7%, removal for decreased drainage 51.9%, removal for complications/other 7.3%.

chunks.title: Quality Gaps and Comparative Effectiveness of Management Strategies for Recurrent Malignant Pleural Effusions
chunks.content: BACKGROUND: Guidelines for recurrent malignant pleural effusions (MPEs) recommend definitive procedures, such as indwelling pleural catheters (IPCs) or pleurodesis, over repeat thoracentesis. We hypothesized that many patients have multiple thoracenteses rather than definitive procedures and that this results in more procedures and complications. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study using SEER-Medicare data from 2007 to 2011. Patients 66 to 90 years of age with an MPE were included. The primary outcome was whether patients with rapidly recurring MPE, defined as recurrence within 2 weeks of first thoracentesis, received guideline consistent care. Guideline consistent care was defined as a definitive second pleural procedure. RESULTS: Thoracentesis for MPE was performed in 23,431 patients. A second pleural procedure because of recurrence was required in 12,967 (55%). Recurrence was rapid in 7,565 (58%) of the 12,967 patients that had a recurrence. Of the 7,565 patients with rapid recurrence, 1,811 (24%) received guideline consistent care. Definitive pleural procedures compared with repeat thoracentesis resulted in fewer subsequent pleural procedures (0.62 vs 1.44 procedures per patient, respectively; P < .0001), fewer pneumothoraxes (< 0.0037 vs 0.009 pneumothoraxes per patient, respectively; P = .001), and fewer ED procedures (0.02 vs 0.04 ED procedures per patient, respectively; P < .001). Repeat thoracentesis and IPCs resulted in fewer inpatient days compared with chest tube or thoracoscopic pleurodesis (0.013 vs 0.013 vs 0.085 vs 0.097 inpatient days per day of life, respectively; P < .001). CONCLUSIONS: Guideline consistent care using definitive procedures compared with repeat thoracentesis was associated with fewer subsequent procedures and complications; however, pleurodesis resulted in more inpatient days.

chunks.title: Quality Gaps and Comparative Effectiveness of Management Strategies for Recurrent Malignant Pleural Effusions
chunks.content: Among 23,431 patients, there were 46,080 thoracenteses, 1,679 IPCs, 1,799 thoracoscopic pleurodeses, and 4,316 chest tube pleurodeses. Median survival from first thoracentesis was 88 days (IQR 26-320). A second pleural procedure occurred in 12,967 (55%); 8,572 (37%) died before any second procedure; 1,892 (8%) were alive without recurrence at last follow-up. Median time to second procedure was 9 days (IQR 3-32). Of those with a second procedure, 10,019 (77%) had repeat thoracentesis and 2,948 (23%) had a definitive procedure. Among 7,565 patients with rapid recurrence (≤14 days), 1,811 (24%) received a definitive second procedure (guideline consistent) and 5,754 (76%) had repeat thoracentesis (guideline inconsistent). Definitive procedures vs repeat thoracentesis were associated with fewer subsequent pleural procedures (0.62 vs 1.44 per patient; P < .0001), fewer pneumothoraces (<0.0037 vs 0.009 per patient; P = .001), and fewer ED procedures (0.02 vs 0.04 per patient; P < .001). Inpatient days per day of life were lower for thoracentesis and IPC compared with chest tube and thoracoscopic pleurodesis (0.013 vs 0.013 vs 0.085 vs 0.097; P < .001). Overall pneumothorax incidence was 711 of 46,080 thoracenteses. Factors independently associated with guideline consistent care included younger age, lung cancer, ED setting for first thoracentesis, involvement of pulmonologists, radiologists, or thoracic surgeons, residence in large metropolitan areas, and later diagnosis years.

chunks.title: Palliative Care and Interventional Pulmonology
chunks.content: This narrative review outlines palliative care needs and interventional pulmonology options for patients with advanced pulmonary diseases, particularly lung cancer and COPD. It summarizes symptom burdens (dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis), advocates early integration of palliative care with disease-directed therapy, and reviews non-interventional measures (opioids, bronchodilators, nonpharmacologic approaches) and interventional strategies such as management of malignant pleural effusions (indwelling pleural catheters vs pleurodesis) and central airway obstruction (debulking, ablation, stenting). Complication profiles and practical considerations are discussed.

chunks.title: Palliative Care and Interventional Pulmonology
chunks.content: Key findings highlighted include: high prevalence of unmet palliative needs in lung cancer and COPD; benefits of early palliative care integration on quality of life and potentially survival; effectiveness of opioids and nonpharmacologic interventions for dyspnea; utility of antibiotics and mucolytics for productive cough and opioids/anesthetics for dry cough; use of tranexamic acid and radiation for hemoptysis. For malignant pleural effusions, indwelling pleural catheters reduce hospitalization days compared with talc pleurodesis and may achieve spontaneous pleurodesis in a subset, with complication rates including empyema, pneumothorax requiring chest tube, cellulitis, and rare infections. For central airway obstruction, mechanical debulking plus ablative therapies and airway stenting can improve symptoms, with device-specific pros and cons.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Narrative review of percutaneous dilational tracheostomy (PDT) covering history, indications, timing, contraindications, training, preparation, and adjuncts (bronchoscopy and ultrasound). Summarizes evidence comparing early vs late tracheostomy and guidance modalities (ultrasound vs bronchoscopy), noting limited trial data and generally similar safety with experienced operators.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Key points: No mortality benefit for early vs late tracheostomy in large RCTs; early placement associated with reduced sedation use but more procedures performed. Two prospective trials compared real-time ultrasound guidance with bronchoscopy for PDT: a small RCT (n=23) found higher rate of initial midline puncture with ultrasound; a larger RCT (n=177) reported longer procedural time and higher desaturation with bronchoscopy, with similar success and complication rates overall. Data on ultrasound remain limited.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Percutaneous dilational tracheostomy (PDT) is widely used in the ICU for airway management in patients with chronic respiratory failure or prolonged mechanical ventilation. Multiple techniques exist, with the single-dilator Ciaglia variant most commonly used. Flexible bronchoscopy is frequently employed as an adjunct and is associated with reduced complications compared with landmark-only techniques. Reported overall complication rates vary, with most being minor, and procedure-related mortality is low. PDT generally compares favorably with surgical tracheostomy with respect to procedure time, complications, and cost.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Across studies summarized, bronchoscopy guidance during PDT was associated with a lower composite complication rate compared with non-bronchoscopic approaches in pooled nonrandomized data (16.8% vs 8.7%). Individual randomized comparisons among PDT techniques reported differences in specific complications (e.g., tracheal ring fracture, bleeding, hypoxemia), but head-to-head data are limited and findings are not uniform. Reported procedure-related mortality ranges from 0% to 0.7%, and bleeding from 0.4% to 8%, mostly minor.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy

chunks.title: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. Indications, care and complications
chunks.content: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) is an effective and safe method for nutritional support in patients with malnutrition and impossibility of oral intake with an estimated survival higher than the months that require enteral nutrition beyond four weeks. The main indications include neoplasms of the upper air-digestive tract and neurological diseases, with dementia currently considered a controversial indication. Anatomical alterations and infectious diseases are the most frequent contraindications. There are different endoscopic techniques; the most widely used being the “pull” method, with a low mortality. Complications are more frequent in patients with multiple pathologies and the elderly. Wound infection, extraction of the tube, tube blockage and bronchoaspiratory pneumonia are the most prevalent complications. Adequate prior preparation of the patient and exhaustive maintenance of the tube can reduce the appearance of these.

chunks.title: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. Indications, care and complications
chunks.content: PEG is favored over parenteral nutrition when the GI tract is functional and enteral nutrition is needed >4 weeks with life expectancy >2 months. Advanced dementia is generally not recommended as an indication. Absolute and relative contraindications are listed. The pull method is most used; gastropexy is preferred in selected cases (e.g., head-and-neck/oesophageal stenoses). Early feeding at 3-6 hours is safe. Complication rates overall range 13-43%, with major complications not exceeding 22%; most frequent are stoma infection, tube dislodgement/obstruction, and aspiration pneumonia. Antibiotic prophylaxis reduces stoma infection; careful antithrombotic management is required.

chunks.title: Percutaneous radiologic gastrostomy versus percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy: A comparison of indications, complications and outcomes in 370 patients
chunks.content: Objective: Percutaneous access to the stomach can be achieved by endoscopic or fluoroscopic methods. Our objective was to compare indications, complications, efficacy and outcomes of these two techniques. Methods: Records of 370 patients with feeding tubes placed either endoscopically by gastroenterology, or fluoroscopically by radiology, at our university-based tertiary care center over a 54-month period were reviewed. Results: 177 gastrostomies were placed endoscopically and 193 fluoroscopically. Nutrition was the most common indication in each group (94 and 92%), but the most common underlying diagnosis was neurologic impairment in the endoscopic group (n = 89, 50%) and malignancy in the fluoroscopic group (n = 134, 69%) (p < 0.001). Complications in the first 30 days were more common with fluoroscopic placement (23% versus 11%, p = 0.002), with infection most frequent. Correlates of late complications were inpatient status (OR 0.26, 95% CI: 0.13-0.51) and a diagnosis of malignancy (OR 2.2, 95% CI: 1.03-4.84). Average follow-up time was 108 days in the fluoroscopic group and 174 days in the endoscopic group. Conclusions: Both endoscopic and fluoroscopic gastrostomy tube placement are safe and effective. Outpatient status was associated with greater early and late complication rates; minor complications such as infection were greater in the fluoroscopic group, while malignancy was associated with late complications.

chunks.title: Percutaneous radiologic gastrostomy versus percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy: A comparison of indications, complications and outcomes in 370 patients
chunks.content: Of 370 patients, 177 received PEG and 193 received PRG. Mean age was 68 ± 15 (PEG) versus 63 ± 14 (PRG). Male sex was 56.5% (PEG) and 59.1% (PRG). Indications were predominantly nutrition (PEG 94.4%, PRG 91.7%). Dysphagia was more common in PEG (67.8% vs 45.6%, p < 0.001); malignancy was more common in PRG (69.4% vs 23.2%, p < 0.001). Inpatient status was more frequent for PEG (91.0% vs 68.9%, p < 0.001). Early complications occurred in 19/177 (10.8%) PEG vs 44/193 (22.8%) PRG (p = 0.038), with early infections in 3/177 vs 14/193 (p = 0.012). Late complications occurred in 17/177 (10.1%) PEG vs 46/193 (23.8%) PRG (p = 0.002), with higher late tube dislodgement (2/177 vs 12/193, p = 0.012) and leakage (1/177 vs 10/193, p = 0.011) in PRG. Major complications: early 2 PEG vs 3 PRG; late 0 PEG vs 1 PRG. No procedure-attributable deaths; mortality reported as 8/177 (4.5%) vs 6/193 (3.1%) within 7 days in table. Logistic regression found outpatient status associated with higher early and late complications, and malignancy associated with late complications (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.03-4.84). Follow-up averaged 174 days (PEG) and 108 days (PRG).

chunks.title: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy: A Practical Overview on Its Indications, Placement Conditions, Management, and Nursing Care
chunks.content: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) feeding represents the most effective and safest option for feeding patients with an impaired or diminished swallowing ability, despite having a functioning digestive system. The use of PEG has evolved to be useful in many situations beyond degenerative neuromuscular disorders, with an increasing body of evidence supporting the advantages of PEG tubes in oncologic and pediatric patients. Risk factors for complications after PEG tube placement include acute and chronic conditions associated with malnutrition and several organic disorders. Patients suitable for PEG tube placement should be individually identified to implement the advantages of this technique while minimizing risk events. The safety of placing a PEG tube in patients under antithrombotic medication has been investigated, as well as the advantages of antibiotic prophylaxis in reducing peristomal infection. Evidence supports the safety of early feeding after placement, thus resulting in lower costs. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy-related complications are rare and mostly prevented by appropriate nursing care. Best medical practice and nursing care will ensure optimal performance leading to a wider acceptance, and greater utility of PEG by healthcare professionals, patients, and caregivers. This review aims to update knowledge relating to PEG tube indications, placement, management, and care in order to reinforce PEG feeding as the most valuable access for patients with a functional gastrointestinal system who have abnormalities in swallowing mechanisms.

chunks.title: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy: A Practical Overview on Its Indications, Placement Conditions, Management, and Nursing Care
chunks.content: PEG is favored over nasogastric feeding due to lower intervention failure rates and comparable or improved safety. In head and neck cancer, prophylactic PEG prior to chemoradiation may limit weight loss, though high-quality evidence remains limited and concerns about prolonged tube dependency exist. In pediatric populations, PEG is efficient and safe, including in small infants, and supports nutritional status across various conditions, including oncology. Absolute contraindications include lack of gastric access (e.g., colonic interposition), massive ascites, uncorrectable coagulopathy, portal hypertension with gastric varices, and obstructing esophageal lesions preventing endoscopic access. Regarding antithrombotics, post-PEG bleeding is uncommon: pooled incidence approximately 2.67% overall and 2.7% without antiplatelet therapy; pooled relative risk with aspirin 1.43 (95% CI 0.89-2.29), clopidogrel 1.21 (95% CI 0.48-3.04), and dual antiplatelet therapy 2.13 (95% CI 0.77-5.91). For infection prevention, peristomal infection without prophylaxis can be up to 32%; prophylactic antibiotics significantly reduce infection risk (pooled odds ratio 0.31; 95% CI 0.22-0.44). Early feeding after PEG appears safe and cost-saving. Prior abdominal surgery is not a contraindication, though gastric surgery may increase technical failure.

chunks.source_file: Performance, long-term management, and coding for percutaneous dilational tracheostomy.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Performance, Long-term Management, and Coding for Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Percutaneous dilatational tracheotomy (PDT) has become widely accepted and can be safely performed by surgeons and nonsurgeons at the ICU bedside. Bedside PDT offers proven clinical outcomes and resource savings, often serving as the tracheostomy procedure of choice for prolonged mechanical ventilation. This article outlines logistics and operations for incorporating PDT into routine ICU care, including team composition, patient selection, procedural steps, bronchoscopy/ultrasound guidance, training and credentialing, documentation, coding, and quality improvement. Evidence comparing PDT to open surgical tracheotomy suggests lower bleeding and mortality with PDT and no significant difference in overall complications, with a trend favoring PDT. Contraindications and special considerations are detailed, particularly for high-risk patients and less experienced operators.

chunks.source_file: Performance, long-term management, and coding for percutaneous dilational tracheostomy.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Performance, Long-term Management, and Coding for Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy
chunks.content: Synthesis of prior evidence indicates PDT is associated with lower bleeding and mortality versus open tracheotomy in a systematic review of 17 randomized controlled trials (1,212 patients). A meta-analysis reported no significant difference in overall complications with a trend favoring percutaneous methods. The American College of Surgeons recommends bedside PDT as the procedure of choice even in high-risk patients. The article provides a practical checklist, outlines absolute and relative contraindications (e.g., age <8 years, gross neck distortion, uncorrectable coagulopathy, PEEP >20 cm H2O), describes team roles, emphasizes bronchoscopy or ultrasound guidance, and recommends training thresholds (≥20 supervised cases and ≥10 annually to maintain competency). Coding guidance includes CPT 31600 for planned tracheostomy (0-day global for Medicare) and related bronchoscopic procedure codes when medically necessary.

chunks.source_file: Physiologic Evaluation of the Patient With Lung Cancer.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Physiologic Evaluation of the Patient With Lung Cancer Being Considered for Resectional Surgery: Diagnosis and Management of Lung Cancer, 3rd ed: American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines
chunks.content: Background: This section of the guidelines provides an evidence-based approach to the preoperative physiologic assessment of a patient being considered for surgical resection of lung cancer. Methods: Current guidelines and medical literature were identified by computerized search and evaluated using standardized methods; recommendations were framed per the ACCP Guidelines Oversight Committee. Results: Assessment should begin with cardiovascular evaluation and spirometry to measure FEV1 and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO). Predicted postoperative (PPO) lung functions should be calculated. If both %PPO FEV1 and %PPO DLCO are >60%, the patient is low risk and no further tests are indicated. If either %PPO FEV1 or %PPO DLCO is between 30% and 60%, a low-technology exercise test (stair climb or shuttle walk) should be performed; satisfactory performance (stair climbing altitude >22 m or shuttle walk distance >400 m) indicates low risk. A cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) is indicated when PPO FEV1 or PPO DLCO (or both) are <30%, or when the low-technology test is not satisfactory. Peak oxygen consumption (O2peak) <10 mL/kg/min or 35% predicted indicates high risk of mortality and long-term disability with major anatomic resection; O2peak >20 mL/kg/min or 75% predicted indicates low risk. Conclusions: Careful preoperative physiologic assessment identifies patients at increased risk with standard lung cancer resection and supports informed decision-making, recognizing that surgery for early-stage lung cancer is the most effective treatment.

chunks.source_file: Physiologic Evaluation of the Patient With Lung Cancer.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Physiologic Evaluation of the Patient With Lung Cancer Being Considered for Resectional Surgery: Diagnosis and Management of Lung Cancer, 3rd ed: American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines
chunks.content: Key recommendations: measure FEV1 and DLCO in all surgical candidates and calculate %PPO values. If both %PPO FEV1 and %PPO DLCO are >60%, no further testing is recommended (low risk). If either is <60% but both are ≥30%, perform a low-technology exercise test (stair climb or shuttle walk); satisfactory performance (stair climb >22 m or shuttle walk >400 m) indicates low risk. If %PPO FEV1 <30% or %PPO DLCO <30%, or if low-technology test performance is unsatisfactory (stair climb <22 m or shuttle walk <400 m), perform CPET. O2max <10 mL/kg/min or <35% predicted denotes high risk for perioperative death and cardiopulmonary complications with major anatomic resection; O2max >20 mL/kg/min or >75% predicted indicates low risk. Additional guidance includes multidisciplinary team assessment, full evaluation regardless of advanced age, preoperative cardiology evaluation for increased cardiovascular risk, repeat PFTs with DLCO after neoadjuvant therapy, combined LVRS and cancer resection for suitable upper-lobe emphysema cases, tobacco dependence treatment for active smokers, and pulmonary rehabilitation for high-risk patients.

chunks.source_file: Pleural controversy  Closed needle pleural bio.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural controversy: Closed needle pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy—Which first?
chunks.content: The most efficient and cost-effective approach to the diagnosis of pleural exudates remains controversial. Important considerations include the respective diagnostic yields of thoracocentesis, closed pleural biopsy and thoracoscopy; the incremental gain in diagnostic yield when sequentially combining these investigations; and the role of various image modalities. The diagnostic yield of thoracocentesis is in the order of 60% for malignancy and >90% for tuberculosis. A second aspiration may increase the yield for malignancy, but a third is generally superfluous. Many authorities consider thoracoscopy the investigation of choice in exudative pleural effusions where a thoracocentesis was nondiagnostic and particularly when malignancy is suspected. It allows for the direct inspection of the pleura and for talc poudrage. Thoracoscopy has a diagnostic yield of 91-95% for malignant disease and as high as 100% for pleural tuberculosis. Access to thoracoscopy is, however, limited in many parts of the world, as significant resources and expertise are required. Blind closed pleural biopsy has a yield of 80% for tuberculosis and <60% for pleural malignancy. Recent studies suggest that CT and/or ultrasound guidance may improve the yield, particularly for malignancy, where it may be as high as 88% and 83%, respectively. A second thoracocentesis combined with an image-assisted pleural biopsy with either an Abrams needle or cutting needle, depending on the setting, may therefore be an acceptable alternative to thoracoscopy. With such an approach, thoracoscopy may potentially be reserved for cases not diagnosed by means of closed pleural biopsy.

chunks.source_file: Pleural controversy  Closed needle pleural bio.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural controversy: Closed needle pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy—Which first?
chunks.content: Key findings summarized: (1) Thoracocentesis: cytology yields approximately 55-60% for malignancy; a second aspiration may add approximately 27% yield while a third adds approximately 5%. For tuberculosis in high-incidence areas, a single thoracocentesis with lymphocytic predominance and elevated ADA can diagnose >90% of cases; pleural fluid smear and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis have sensitivities <50%. Ultrasound guidance improves success (up to 97%) and reduces pneumothorax risk. (2) Thoracoscopy: medical thoracoscopy yields 91-95% for malignant disease and up to 100% for pleural tuberculosis; major complications occur in 2-3% and mortality approximately 0.4%; addition of cytology or blind biopsy to thoracoscopy adds approximately 1% yield for malignancy. (3) Closed needle pleural biopsy: blind Abrams-type biopsy yields <60% for malignancy and approximately 80% for tuberculosis (up to 87% with ≥6 specimens). Image guidance improves performance: ultrasound-guided cutting needle biopsy yields up to 87% for all pleural pathologies (77% malignancy); ultrasound-assisted Abrams biopsy had higher tissue adequacy than ultrasound-assisted Tru-cut in one randomized study (91.0% vs 78.7%, P = 0.015) and higher yield for tuberculosis (81.8% vs 65.2%, P = 0.022), with comparable yields for malignancy (Abrams 83.3%). CT-guided pleural biopsy shows sensitivity around 87% for pleural thickening and up to 93% for mesothelioma; in randomized comparison, CT-guided Abrams biopsy sensitivity 87.5% vs thoracoscopy 94.1% (P = 0.252), with similar performance when pleural thickening ≥10 mm.

chunks.source_file: Pleural Cryobiopsy A Systematic Review and Met.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural Cryobiopsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
chunks.content: BACKGROUND: Pleural biopsy using either video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery or medical pleuroscopy is the current diagnostic criterion standard for pleural pathology with a high, yet imperfect, diagnostic yield. Cryobiopsy may provide greater tissue, increase depth of sampled tissue, and/or reduce crush artifact. However, its impact on diagnostic yield remains uncertain, and there are potential concerns regarding its safety too. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the same. METHODS: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, and Google Scholar for studies evaluating the performance of pleural cryobiopsy, assessing the quality of each study using the Quality Assessment, Data Abstraction and Synthesis-2 tool. Using inverse variance weighting, we performed a meta-analysis of diagnostic yield estimations. We also reviewed specimen characteristics and complications related to the procedure. RESULTS: Seven observational studies involving 586 pleural biopsies (311 cryobiopsies and 275 flexible forceps biopsies) were evaluated. All but one study used a semi-rigid thoracoscope. Meta-analysis generated a diagnostic yield of 96.5% for cryobiopsy and 93.1% for forceps biopsy with an inverse variance-weighted OR of 1.61 (95% CI, 0.71-3.66) and an I2 of 16%. No instances of moderate to severe bleeding were reported with cryobiopsy. A funnel plot illustrated no major publication bias. CONCLUSIONS: Based on analysis of relatively homogenous observational data, pleural cryobiopsy is safe but does not increase diagnostic yield over flexible forceps biopsy. Adequately powered multicenter randomized trials are needed for further investigation.

chunks.source_file: Pleural Cryobiopsy A Systematic Review and Met.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural Cryobiopsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
chunks.content: Seven observational studies representing 586 biopsies (311 cryobiopsies and 275 flexible forceps biopsies) were analyzed. Most studies used a semi-rigid thoracoscope; one used a rigid thoracoscope but only flexible forceps and cryoprobe data were included for consistency. In all but one study, both cryobiopsy and flexible forceps biopsy were performed in the same patient. Meta-analysis yielded a pooled diagnostic yield of 96.5% for cryobiopsy and 93.1% for flexible forceps biopsy, with an inverse variance-weighted odds ratio of 1.61 (95% CI, 0.71-3.66), I2 = 16%, and overall effect z = 1.15, P = .25. Studies consistently showed larger specimen sizes with cryobiopsy and, where assessed, fewer instances of crush artifact. None of the studies reported any instances of major bleeding with cryobiopsy. A funnel plot showed no obvious publication bias.

chunks.source_file: Pleural Interventions in the Management of Hep.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural Interventions in the Management of Hepatic Hydrothorax
chunks.content: Hepatic hydrothorax (HH) occurs in 5%-15% of patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension and reflects advanced liver disease. Presentations range from small, minimally symptomatic effusions to massive effusions with respiratory failure. High-quality HH-specific evidence is limited. This case-based review summarizes pleural intervention options—thoracentesis, tube thoracostomy, indwelling tunneled pleural catheter (IPC), pleurodesis, and surgical approaches—and provides practical recommendations. Multidisciplinary management with hepatology and transplant teams is emphasized. For non-transplant candidates with refractory HH, IPC is suggested for palliation when appropriate; serial thoracentesis is recommended when definitive procedures are not possible. For transplant candidates, serial thoracentesis is commonly used while the potential role of IPC is considered within the transplant evaluation.

chunks.source_file: Pleural Interventions in the Management of Hep.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Pleural Interventions in the Management of Hepatic Hydrothorax
chunks.content: Key data summarized: serial thoracentesis is standard but associated with cumulative complications in HH populations; chest tube drainage in HH is linked with poor outcomes and higher mortality than thoracentesis in database studies; TIPS benefits many but up to 25% have partial or no response; IPC can palliate symptoms with variable spontaneous pleurodesis and notable infection risks. Illustrative studies include: Yoon 2019 (12-month mortality: thoracentesis 18.2% [2/11], pigtail catheter 87.5% [14/16], surgery with diaphragmatic repair/pleurodesis 70.0% [7/10]); Orman & Lok 2009 (chest tube n=17 with 35.3% mortality at 3 months [6/17]); IPC series report pleurodesis and infection rates (e.g., Chen 2016: pleurodesis 33% [8/24], infection 16.7% [4/24], IPC-related mortality 0%).

chunks.content: Letter describing two cases of ventricular fibrillation occurring seconds after endobronchial epinephrine (5 ml, 1:20,000) instillation via guide sheath for severe bleeding during EBUS-guided transbronchial lung biopsy. Both patients had no identified cardiac risk factors, were resuscitated with cardioversion, and recovered. Authors question efficacy and safety of endobronchial epinephrine for biopsy-related bleeding and advise against administering epinephrine into the lung periphery via guide sheath.

chunks.content: Both patients received epinephrine 0.25 mg endobronchially. Ventricular fibrillation developed within seconds, requiring cardioversion (150 J and 250 J). Electrolytes and subsequent cardiac evaluations were normal. No deaths occurred. Authors note literature reports of serious cardiac events with low-dose epinephrine and the rarity of fatal bleeding after TBLB.

chunks.title: Preoperative endobronchial photodynamic therapy improves resectability in initially irresectable (inoperable) locally advanced non small cell lung cancer
chunks.content: Objectives: Prospective randomized trial to assess effectiveness and safety of neoadjuvant photodynamic therapy (PDT) plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone, and the possibility for subsequent surgery in locally advanced NSCLC. Methods: Patients with stage IIIA/IIIB central NSCLC (main bronchus/distal trachea involvement) initially unresectable or functionally inoperable but potentially operable after neoadjuvant therapy were randomized to chemotherapy plus endobronchial PDT or chemotherapy alone, followed by surgery. PDT used chlorine E6 (Radachlorin) and 662 nm laser light before each of three chemotherapy cycles. Results: 42 patients were randomized (21 per arm). Groups were similar at baseline. No major PDT complications were observed. Partial response occurred in 19/21 (90%) with PDT and 16/21 (76%) without (p = 0.460 in abstract; radiologic partial response p = 0.158 in text). These patients underwent thoracotomy; unresectable tumor at thoracotomy occurred in 3 patients in the No-PDT arm. There were 14 pneumonectomies and 5 lobectomies in the PDT arm vs 10 pneumonectomies and 3 lobectomies in the No-PDT arm. R0 resection was higher with PDT (89%) vs No-PDT (54%) (p = 0.038). Conclusions: Neoadjuvant PDT with chemotherapy is effective, safe, and improves resectability and resection completeness in stage III central NSCLC.

chunks.title: Preoperative endobronchial photodynamic therapy improves resectability in initially irresectable (inoperable) locally advanced non small cell lung cancer
chunks.content: 42 patients randomized (PDT n = 21; No-PDT n = 21); baseline balanced for age, sex, ECOG, stage IIIA/IIIB, histology. Reasons for initial unresectability/inoperability included tracheal involvement (n = 19), functional intolerance to pneumonectomy (n = 10), T4 mediastinal invasion (n = 6), multiple N2 (n = 5), N3 (n = 2). FEV1 at baseline: 69 ± 17% predicted (PDT) vs 71 ± 19% (No-PDT). PDT sessions averaged 11.5 min (range 9-14). PDT complications: hemoptysis in 2/21 (10%), minor. Chemotherapy completed in 36/42 (86%); discontinuations in 6 (3 per group) due to toxicity (n = 5) or progression (n = 1). Partial radiographic response: 19/21 (90%) vs 16/21 (76%), p = 0.158; endoscopic CR: 7/21 (33%) vs 2/21 (10%), p = 0.054; fewer non-responders with PDT. In functionally inoperable patients (PDT 6; No-PDT 4), FEV1 modestly improved; 5/6 (PDT) and 3/4 (No-PDT) underwent lobectomy instead of pneumonectomy due to main bronchus tumor disappearance. Tracheal recanalization in those with initial tracheal involvement: 9/9 (100%) PDT vs 7/10 (70%) No-PDT, p = 0.124. Thoracotomy performed in 19 (PDT) and 16 (No-PDT); resections achieved in 19 and 13, respectively; exploratory thoracotomy 0 vs 3, p = 0.086. R0 resection among resections: 17/19 (89%) PDT vs 7/13 (54%) No-PDT, p = 0.038; all R1 margins involved bronchial stump; no R2. Post-surgery deaths: 1 per group (pneumonia in PDT; COPD exacerbation in No-PDT), both after pneumonectomy. One tracheobronchial anastomosis failure in PDT, treated conservatively.

chunks.source_file: Prospective study to determine the volume of p.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Prospective Study To Determine the Volume of Pleural Fluid Required To Diagnose Malignancy
chunks.content: Background: The optimal volume of pleural fluid to diagnose a malignant effusion is unknown. Our study was designed to demonstrate if a minimum pleural fluid volume (10 mL) is equivalent to a large volume thoracentesis to make a cytopathologic diagnosis of malignancy. Methods: A total of 121 thoracentesis samples were obtained from 102 patients with suspected or known malignant effusions. Pleural fluid was collected in three aliquots for cytologic examination (10 mL, 60 mL, ≥150 mL). The pathologist was blinded to patient identifiers and aliquot volume. Sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value (NPV), and positive predictive value (PPV) were calculated for each volume for the diagnosis of malignancy. Results: Pleural malignancy was diagnosed in 90 patient encounters (74.4%). For direct smear/cytospin, there was increased sensitivity and NPV for 60 mL (P = .0058 and P = .045, respectively) and for ≥150 mL (P < .001 and P = .009, respectively) compared with 10 mL. For combined direct smear/cytospin and cell block preparations, statistical significance for sensitivity and NPV existed only between the 10 mL and ≥150 mL specimens (P = .0099 and P = .033, respectively). No statistical difference existed for specificity or PPV for any aliquot volume. Conclusions: The sensitivity for diagnosis of pleural malignancy is dependent on the pleural fluid volume extracted during thoracentesis. Volumes of 10 mL do not perform as well as larger volumes. When both direct smear/cytospin and cell block preparations are used, we recommend ≥150 mL, whereas when only direct smear/cytospin is used, 60 mL is adequate for the diagnosis of a malignant pleural effusion.

chunks.content: Of 121 thoracentesis encounters, 90 (74.3%) had malignant pleural effusions by the reference standard. After excluding 3 encounters with missing slides, 118 encounters remained, with 87 (73.7%) malignant. For direct smear/cytospin-only analyses including encounters with results for all three volumes (n=107; 78 malignant), sensitivity increased with volume: 10 mL 48.7% (38/78), 60 mL 62.8% (49/78), ≥150 mL 69.2% (54/78). Pairwise sensitivity differences were significant for 10 vs 60 mL (P = .0058) and 10 vs ≥150 mL (P < .001); 60 vs ≥150 mL was not significant (P = .090). NPV also increased: 10 mL 41.2% (28/68), 60 mL 47.3% (26/55), ≥150 mL 51.0% (25/49), with significant differences for 10 vs 60 mL (P = .045) and 10 vs ≥150 mL (P = .009). Specificity and PPV did not differ significantly across volumes. For combined direct smear/cytospin plus cell block (n=71; 54 malignant), sensitivity was 75.9% (41/54) at 10 mL, 79.6% (43/54) at 60 mL, and 87.0% (47/54) at ≥150 mL; 10 vs ≥150 mL was significant (P = .0099). NPV was 55.2% (16/29), 59.3% (16/27), and 66.7% (17/21), respectively; 10 vs ≥150 mL was significant (P = .033). Specificity and PPV showed no significant differences. Cancer types among malignant effusions included lung adenocarcinoma (31/90), metastatic breast carcinoma (24/90), and others.

chunks.source_file: Rahman-2015-Effect of Opioids vs NSAIDs and La.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Effect of Opioids vs NSAIDs and Larger vs Smaller Chest Tube Size on Pain Control and Pleurodesis Efficacy Among Patients With Malignant Pleural Effusion: The TIME1 Randomized Clinical Trial
chunks.content: IMPORTANCE: NSAIDs are often avoided in malignant pleural effusion (MPE) pleurodesis due to concern for reduced efficacy; smaller chest tubes may be less painful but their pleurodesis efficacy is uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To assess effects of analgesia (NSAIDs vs opiates) and chest tube size (12F vs 24F) on pain and pleurodesis efficacy. DESIGN, SETTING, PARTICIPANTS: Multicenter 2×2 factorial phase 3 randomized clinical trial at 16 hospitals (UK, US, Canada), 2007-2013, enrolling 320 adults needing pleurodesis for symptomatic MPE. INTERVENTIONS: Thoracoscopy patients (n=206) all received 24F tubes and were randomized to NSAIDs vs opiates; non-thoracoscopy patients (n=114) were randomized to NSAIDs vs opiates and to 12F vs 24F tubes. MAIN OUTCOMES: Mean pain (0-100 mm VAS) while chest tube in situ (superiority) and pleurodesis failure at 3 months (need for further ipsilateral pleural intervention; noninferiority margin 15%). RESULTS: Pain did not differ between opiates (n=150; mean 23.8 mm) and NSAIDs (n=144; mean 22.1 mm; adjusted difference -1.5 mm; 95% CI -5.0 to 2.0; P=0.40). NSAID group required more rescue analgesia (26.3% vs 38.1%; rate ratio 2.1; 95% CI 1.3-3.4; P=0.003). Pleurodesis failure occurred in 30/150 (20%) with opiates and 33/144 (23%) with NSAIDs, meeting noninferiority (1-sided 95% CI lower bound -10%; P=0.004). Pain was lower with 12F vs 24F tubes (22.0 mm vs 26.8 mm; adjusted difference -6.0 mm; 95% CI -11.7 to -0.2; P=0.04). Pleurodesis failure was higher with 12F vs 24F (30% vs 24%); noninferiority not met (1-sided 95% CI lower bound -20%; P=0.14). CONCLUSIONS: NSAIDs provided similar pain control to opiates and were noninferior for pleurodesis efficacy at 3 months but required more rescue medication. Smaller tubes modestly reduced pain but did not meet noninferiority for pleurodesis efficacy.

chunks.content: 320 patients randomized (160 NSAIDs, 160 opiates); 206 underwent thoracoscopy (all 24F), 114 non-thoracoscopy randomized to 12F (n=57) or 24F (n=57) tubes. Pain outcome available in 308/320 (96%); pleurodesis outcomes available in 294/320 (ITT primary analysis). Analgesia comparison: Mean pain VAS similar between opiates (n=150; 23.8 mm) and NSAIDs (n=144; 22.1 mm); adjusted difference -1.5 mm (95% CI -5.0 to 2.0; P=0.40). Pleurodesis failure by 3 months occurred in 30/150 (20%) opiates and 33/144 (23%) NSAIDs; noninferiority met (1-sided 95% CI lower bound -10%; P=0.004). Tube size comparison (non-thoracoscopy patients): Pain lower with 12F vs 24F (n=54 vs n=56; means 22.0 vs 26.8 mm); adjusted difference -6.0 mm (95% CI -11.7 to -0.2; P=0.04). Pleurodesis failure higher with 12F vs 24F (30% vs 24%); noninferiority not met (1-sided 95% CI lower bound -20%; P=0.14).
