chunks.title: Transbronchial Cryobiopsy in Interstitial Lung Diseases: State-of-the-Art Review for the Interventional Pulmonologist
chunks.content: Interstitial lung diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders that are often difficult to diagnose precisely. Clinical, laboratory, radiographic, and histologic information may be needed to arrive at the correct diagnosis. The multidisciplinary discussion has been proven to be useful in this patient group. Transbronchial cryobiopsy has become a popular method for obtaining tissue samples. Over the last decade, substantial research has assessed the feasibility, safety, and diagnostic endpoints of transbronchial cryobiopsy in patients with interstitial lung disease. Data continue to mount to support its use, reflected in guidelines and expert panel reports. Patient selection, procedural performance, and appropriate specimen handling are critical for success. A coordinated approach by pulmonologists with expertise in interstitial lung diseases, interventional pulmonologists, and thoracic pathologists is essential. This evidence-based narrative review addresses transbronchial cryobiopsies from these three perspectives and uses current literature to address nine common procedural questions.

chunks.title: Transbronchial Cryobiopsy in Interstitial Lung Diseases: State-of-the-Art Review for the Interventional Pulmonologist
chunks.content: Meta-analyses report acceptable diagnostic yield for transbronchial cryobiopsy (TBC) in diffuse parenchymal lung disease: Sethi et al. analyzed 27 studies (1443 patients) with an overall yield of 72.9%; Sharp et al. (11 studies, 704 patients) reported 84.4%; Johannson et al. (11 studies, 731 patients) reported a pooled estimate of 79% (range 74%-98%); Ravaglia et al. (15 studies, 781 patients) reported 81%; the 2019 ACCP Guideline pooled estimate was 82.5%. In multidisciplinary discussion (MDD), adding TBC histology increased highly confident IPF diagnosis from 29% to 63% in a cohort of 117 fibrotic ILD patients (+34%). In a prospective multicenter study with sequential TBC and SLB, TBC-sourced information was useful to MDD in 48 of 65 patients (75%). Diagnostic concordance between TBC and SLB varied: an early prospective study found full histologic concordance in 8 of 21 cases (38%); a larger multicenter study reported raw agreement between TBC and SLB of 70.8% for guideline-refined pattern (weighted κ 0.70, 95% CI 0.55-0.86), 69.2% for specific histologic pattern (κ 0.47, 0.30-0.64), and 76.9% for final MDD diagnosis (κ 0.62, 0.47-0.78). Safety signals favored TBC: hospital length of stay was longer with SLB (6.1 vs 2.6 days). Mortality due to adverse events was higher with SLB than TBC (2.7% vs 0.3%). Elective SLB in-hospital mortality was 1.7% (nonelective 16%). SLB 30-day mortality up to 16.7% was observed in a single-center series of patients ultimately diagnosed with UIP. TBC 30-day mortality ranged 0%-4.0%; 90-day mortality 2.5% in one report; meta-analysis procedural mortality 0.3%; ACCP estimated 0.5%. TBC pneumothorax and severe bleeding were estimated at <10% and 0.3%, respectively; SLB bleeding was infrequent and often minimal (<20 mL).

chunks.title: Transbronchial Lung Cryobiopsy and Video-assisted Thoracoscopic Lung Biopsy in the Diagnosis of Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease: A Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy
chunks.content: Rationale: Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is increasingly being used for the assessment of diffuse parenchymal lung diseases. Several studies have shown larger biopsy samples and higher yields compared with conventional transbronchial biopsies. However, the higher risk of bleeding and other complications has raised concerns for widespread use of this modality. Objectives: To study the diagnostic accuracy and safety profile of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy and compare with video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) by reviewing available evidence from the literature. Methods: Medline and PubMed were searched from inception until December 2016. Data on diagnostic performance were abstracted by constructing two-by-two contingency tables for each study. Data on a priori selected safety outcomes were collected. Risk of bias was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies tool. Random effects meta-analyses were performed to obtain summary estimates of the diagnostic accuracy. Results: The pooled diagnostic yield, pooled sensitivity, and pooled specificity of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy were 83.7% (76.9-88.8%), 87% (85-89%), and 57% (40-73%), respectively. The pooled diagnostic yield, pooled sensitivity, and pooled specificity of VATS were 92.7% (87.6-95.8%), 91.0% (89-92%), and 58% (31-81%), respectively. The incidence of grade 2 (moderate to severe) endobronchial bleeding after transbronchial lung cryobiopsy and of post-procedural pneumothorax was 4.9% (2.2-10.7%) and 9.5% (5.9-14.9%), respectively. Conclusions: Although the diagnostic test accuracy measures of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy lag behind those of VATS, with an acceptable safety profile and potential cost savings, the former could be considered as an alternative in the evaluation of patients with diffuse parenchymal lung diseases.

VATS: pooled diagnostic yield 92.7% (95% CI 87.6-95.8%; I2 85%), pooled sensitivity 91% (95% CI 89-92%; I2 91%), pooled specificity 58% (95% CI 31-81%; I2 0%), DOR 21.06 (95% CI 7.08-62.60). SROC AUC 0.85 (SE 0.07). Safety after TLCB: grade 2 (moderate to severe) endobronchial bleeding 4.9% (95% CI 2.2-10.7%); pneumothorax 9.5% (95% CI 5.9-14.9%).

chunks.title: Treatment of Pulmonary Carcinoid Tumors With Bronchoscopic Cryotherapy: A 28-Year Single-center Experience
chunks.content: Background: Pulmonary carcinoids are rare tumors originating from neuroendocrine cells in the lungs. Because of their potentially infiltrative nature, surgical resection remains the treatment of choice. However, not all patients with technically resectable disease will be able to undergo surgery, primarily because of poor lung function or medical co-morbidities. Centrally located, intraluminal tumors have been reported to be amenable to bronchoscopic treatment. We specifically examined the role of cryotherapy in the treatment of bronchial carcinoid tumors. Methods: Sixty-three patients (52.38% female) who underwent a combined total of 243 cryotherapy procedures for treatment of bronchial carcinoid between 1992 and 2020 in our institution were included. Following multidisciplinary discussion, patients were considered for first-line cryotherapy when lung resection was deemed not possible or when they had rejected surgery. Results: Cryotherapy resulted in complete remission in 21 (33.33%) patients with maximum tumor diameter less than 20 mm (mean 11.08 mm, 95% CI 8.76-13.40), and allowed 22 (34.92%) patients with larger lesions (mean 24.04 mm, 95% CI 18.78-29.30) to proceed with parenchymal sparing resections. Marked symptomatic relief (P < 0.001) was reported by 58 (92.06%) patients. Median follow-up was 33 months (range 0-243). One (1.59%) patient had recurrence in a contralateral lobe 3 years after surgery and was treated with radiofrequency ablation. Conclusions: We provide evidence on the safety and efficacy of cryotherapy and encourage wider adoption of this inexpensive and minimally invasive technique for treatment of bronchial carcinoids.

chunks.title: Treatment of Pulmonary Carcinoid Tumors With Bronchoscopic Cryotherapy: A 28-Year Single-center Experience
chunks.content: Sixty-three patients (52.38% female), median age 48 years (range 17-88), received first-line cryotherapy when considered inoperable (69.84%) or if they refused surgery (7.93%). Typical carcinoid in 58 (92.06%) and atypical in 5 (7.93%). Tumor location: main bronchus 20 (31.75%), bronchus intermedius 15 (23.81%), lobar bronchus 28 (44.44%). Median cryotherapy applications per patient were 3 (range 1-18); median interval between procedures 35 days (range 6-3556). Bronchoscopic cryotherapy resulted in marked symptomatic relief in 58 (92.06%) patients who had undergone 3 or fewer cryoablations (P < 0.001). No immediate or late postprocedural complications occurred; all patients were discharged the same day; none required re-admission. Transient cough with blood-stained sputum resolved within 3-5 days. Complete tumor removal with cryotherapy alone occurred in 18 (28.57%) patients with typical carcinoid; an additional 3 patients who underwent surgery had no residual tumor on final histology, totaling 21 (33.33%) with complete remission attributable to cryotherapy. Thirty-two (50.79%) patients underwent surgery after cryotherapy; tumor size reduction was achieved in 29/32 and 22 (34.92% overall) underwent bronchoplastic/sleeve parenchymal-sparing resections; none required more extensive resection than initially anticipated and 13 ultimately required lesser procedures, avoiding 9 pneumonectomies and 4 bilobectomies. Median follow-up for survivors as of July 2020 was 33 months (range 0-243). One patient had contralateral lobe recurrence 3 years after surgery, managed with radiofrequency ablation.

chunks.title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials and Meta-Analysis
chunks.content: Introduction: Percutaneous dilational tracheostomy (PDT) is a common and increasingly used procedure in the intensive care unit (ICU). It is usually performed with bronchoscopy guidance. Ultrasound has emerged as a useful tool in order to assist PDT, potentially improving its success rate and reducing procedural-related complications. Objective: To investigate whether the ultrasound-guided PDT is equivalent or superior to the bronchoscopy-guided or anatomical landmarks-guided PDT with regard to procedural-related and clinical complications. Methods: A systematic review of randomized clinical trials was conducted comparing an ultrasound-guided PDT to the control groups (either a bronchoscopy-guided PDT or an anatomical landmark- guided PDT) in patients undergoing a PDT in the ICU. The primary outcome was the incidence of major procedural-related and clinical complication rates. The secondary outcome was the incidence of minor complication rates. Random-effect meta-analyzes were used to pool the results. Results: Four studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and they were analyzed. The studies included 588 participants. There were no differences in the major complication rates between the patients who were assigned to the ultrasound-guided PDT when compared to the control groups (pooled risk ratio [RR]: 0.48; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.13-1.71, I2 = 0%). The minor complication rates were not different between the groups, but they had a high heterogeneity (pooled RR: 0.49; 95% CI 0.16-1.50; I2 = 85%). The sensitivity analyzes that only included the randomized controlled trials that used a landmark-guided PDT as the control group showed lower rates of minor complications in the ultrasound-guided PDT group (pooled RR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.31-0.98, I2 = 0%). Conclusion: The ultrasound-guided PDT seems to be safe and it is comparable to the bronchoscopy-guided PDT regarding the major and minor procedural-related or clinical complications. It also seems to reduce the minor

chunks.title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Dilational Tracheostomy: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials and Meta-Analysis
chunks.content: Four single-center unblinded RCTs (n=588 randomized; n=561 analyzed) were included: two compared ultrasound-guided to anatomical landmark-guided PDT and two compared ultrasound-guided to bronchoscopy-guided PDT. Ultrasound guidance was real-time in all trials; three used the Griggs forceps dilator technique and one used the Ciaglia single dilator technique. Major complications: 10/561 (1.8%) overall; pooled RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.13-1.71; I2=0%), not significantly different between ultrasound-guided and controls. Minor complications: pooled rate 19.2% with high heterogeneity; pooled RR 0.49 (95% CI 0.16-1.50; I2=86%), not significantly different overall. Sensitivity analysis limited to landmark-guided controls showed fewer minor complications with ultrasound guidance (pooled RR 0.49; 95% CI 0.25-0.96; I2=0%). Procedure duration was reported in three trials; ultrasound guidance was generally faster, with a statistically significant difference in Yavuz et al. (18.6 ± 6.3 vs 24.1 ± 8.0 minutes; P = .001). Additional procedural metrics favored ultrasound in individual trials (fewer multiple attempts; higher first-pass success). Risk of bias: all studies unblinded; random sequence generation and allocation concealment clearly reported in two trials; funnel plot did not suggest publication bias.

chunks.content: Over the last decade, endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) evolved into a validated and powerful diagnostic tool. Although it is integral to medical care in some health-care systems, others struggle to justify its purchase based on diminishing reimbursement. In analyzing its value to a health-care system, looking at procedural reimbursement alone will grossly underestimate its economic impact. Downstream revenue has been defined by administrators as revenue captured after patients use one hospital service and then use others. By analyzing consecutive EBUS cases and taking downstream revenue into account, 2400000 in collections was attributed to 97 patients who were newly referred for this procedure.

chunks.title: Unimodality and Multimodality Cryodebridement for Airway Obstruction: A Single-Center Experience with Safety and Efficacy
chunks.content: Rationale: Cryodebridement (CD) refers to the removal of obstructive material from the lumen of the tracheobronchial tree by freezing with a cryoprobe, which is usually inserted through a flexible bronchoscope. This method of achieving instant recanalization of airways has been established for over 20 years, but published experience comprises limited case series. Objectives: This study describes a single large-volume referral center experience, including clinical outcomes and safety profile. Methods: Electronic medical records of 156 patients who underwent bronchoscopic CD between December 2007 and March 2012 as the primary method to relieve airway obstruction were reviewed retrospectively. Measurements and Main Results: The most frequent cause of airway obstruction was malignancy (n = 88), with non-small-cell lung cancer and metastatic renal cell carcinoma being the most common etiologies. The site of obstruction was localized to the central airways in 63 patients (40%) and the distal airways in 44 patients (28%), and it was diffuse in 49 patients (32%). Bronchoscopic airway patency was achieved in 95% of patients, with the highest success rates found in those with obstruction localized in the central airways. Improvement in symptoms occurred in 118 (82%) of 144 symptomatic patients. Serious complications were reported in 17 patients (11%) and included respiratory distress, severe bleeding, airway injury, and hemodynamic instability. All patients responded to treatment, and no intra- or postoperative deaths were reported. Conclusions: CD, when used alone or in combination with other endoscopic treatment modalities, appears to be safe and effective in treating endoluminal airway obstruction.

chunks.title: Unimodality and Multimodality Cryodebridement for Airway Obstruction: A Single-Center Experience with Safety and Efficacy
chunks.content: A total of 156 patients (mean age 63 years; range 21-88; 1:1 male:female) underwent CD. Most were symptomatic at presentation (144/156, 92%); 31 (20%) were initially admitted to ICU. Obstruction location: central 63 (40%), distal 44 (28%), diffuse 49 (32%). Lesion type: endobronchial 66 (42%), mixed 90 (58%). Etiology: malignant 88 (56%)—with non-small-cell lung cancer 49 (31%), renal cell carcinoma 19 (12%)—and benign 68 (44%), with granulation tissue 40 (26%) the most common benign cause. Airway patency (complete or partial) was achieved in 148/156 (95%) overall. By location: central complete 52/63 (83%), partial 10/63 (16%), none 1/63 (2%); distal complete 24/44 (55%), partial 16/44 (36%), none 4/44 (9%); diffuse complete 19/49 (39%), partial 27/49 (55%), none 3/49 (6%). Symptom improvement occurred in 118/144 (82%) symptomatic patients. Second bronchoscopy within 4 weeks was performed in 35/156 (22%); partial-to-complete patency achieved in 32/35 (91%) after the second procedure; 2 additional patients improved after a third procedure within 4 weeks. Removal of foreign bodies, mucus plugs, and blood clots was successful in 100% after the first bronchoscopy. Median procedure duration 63 minutes (SD 35; range 11-225). Concomitant procedures: forceps debridement 79 (51%), electrocautery 47 (30%), APC 27 (17%), balloon dilation 39 (25%), stent placement 19 (12%), photodynamic therapy 9 (6%). CD alone was used in 42 (27%). Radiologic improvement on CT within 8 weeks noted in 41/70 (59%) who had follow-up imaging. Complications: moderate bleeding in 6 patients, a partial mucosal tear in 1 patient (no repair required), respiratory distress requiring ETI in 7 patients, NIV used in 2 patients. No pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. All patients recovered; no procedure-related deaths. Overall, serious complications occurred in 17 patients (11%).

chunks.title: Update on tracheobronchial anatomy and flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy in thoracic anesthesia
chunks.content: Purpose of review: To review tracheobronchial anatomy and the use of flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy in thoracic anesthesia. Recent findings: Mastery of tracheobronchial anatomy is essential for correct placement of lung isolation devices (double-lumen endotracheal tubes and bronchial blockers). Anatomical changes occur with aging and in COPD, affecting tracheal position and diameters, and must be recognized to optimize device placement. Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy is emphasized as a key skill for confirming and optimizing placement of lung isolation devices and for interventional procedures. Summary: Familiarity with airway anatomy and fiberoptic techniques is fundamental to safe and effective management of patients undergoing thoracic anesthesia.

chunks.content: Key anatomical parameters summarized include tracheal length (~15 cm), tracheal diameter averages (men ~22 mm, women ~19 mm), cricoid as the narrowest portion (men ~17 mm, women ~13 mm), and key bronchial distances (carina to right upper lobe take-off ~2.0 cm in men, ~1.5 cm in women; carina to left upper/lower bifurcation ~5.0 cm in men, ~4.5 cm in women). Age and COPD can shift the trachea (often rightward) and alter tracheal dimensions. A systematic bronchoscopy exam is described, including recognition of the right upper lobe trifurcation as a landmark distinguishing right from left bronchus. Evidence cited indicates auscultation/clamping alone can yield a high malposition rate for DLTs (reported up to 35%), whereas fiberoptic confirmation allows correction of malpositions. Practical steps and optimal positions for right- and left-sided DLTs and bronchial blockers are detailed, including cuff positioning relative to the carina and considerations when the right upper lobe take-off is close to the carina. Additional uses include guidance for endobronchial stent placement and post-airway-exchange catheter examinations.

chunks.title: Use of fibrinolytics and deoxyribonuclease in adult patients with pleural empyema: a consensus statement
chunks.content: This international consensus statement addresses the use of intrapleural fibrinolytic and deoxyribonuclease (DNase) therapy in adult patients with bacterial empyema. An expert panel of 22 clinicians from 20 institutions across five countries developed seven graded and four ungraded recommendations using a systematic literature review (83 studies) and a modified Delphi process. Key recommendations include avoiding DNase monotherapy and not using fibrinolytic monotherapy as first-line therapy; when intrapleural therapy is used, combination tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) plus DNase is recommended. Suggested dosing is tPA 10 mg twice daily and DNase 5 mg twice daily, administered concurrently with 1 h of chest tube clamping. The number of doses should be individualized based on clinical and imaging response. Guidance is provided on use in patients with coagulopathy/antithrombotics, timing relative to surgery, and selective use of saline irrigation when fibrinolytics are contraindicated.

chunks.title: Use of fibrinolytics and deoxyribonuclease in adult patients with pleural empyema: a consensus statement
chunks.content: Consensus recommendations were: avoid DNase monotherapy (strong recommendation, low certainty) and avoid first-line fibrinolytic monotherapy (weak recommendation, moderate certainty). For intrapleural therapy, use combined tPA and DNase (strong recommendation, moderate certainty). Suggested dosing is DNase 5 mg twice daily and tPA 10 mg twice daily, given concurrently, with chest tube clamping for at least 1 hour post-dose. Dosing should be individualized to clinical and radiographic response. Hold therapeutic anticoagulation and non-aspirin antiplatelets when feasible; avoid fibrinolytics in significant coagulopathy unless corrected. Combination therapy can be initial or subsequent therapy based on local expertise and surgical availability; consider a VATS-first approach for suspected organized (stage 3) empyema. Cost should not drive choice between intrapleural therapy and primary surgery in the absence of evidence. Saline irrigation may be considered only when fibrinolytics are contraindicated and the patient is not a surgical candidate. Evidence cited includes MIST1 (n=454) showing no benefit for streptokinase vs placebo, and MIST2 (n=210) showing improved drainage, reduced surgical referral, and shorter hospital stay with combined tPA+DNase. Comparative data include higher haemothorax with tPA+DNase vs urokinase (7/41 vs 0/52; p=0.002) and higher serious bleeding with alteplase vs urokinase in another RCT (5/18 and 4/33 vs 0/48).

chunks.title: Expert Statement: Pneumothorax Associated with Endoscopic Valve Therapy for Emphysema - Potential Mechanisms, Treatment Algorithm, and Case Examples
chunks.content: The use of endoscopically placed unidirectional valves for the treatment of emphysema is increasing. With better patient selection, there is also an increased likelihood of complications associated with the procedure, such as postprocedural pneumothorax. There is, however, little evidence of pneumothorax management in patients with severe COPD and emphysema. This report describes an expert recommendation that has been developed to outline pneumothorax management after valve placement to inform physicians and patients of the risk-benefit profile and to assist them in decision making. Skilled and aggressive pneumothorax management is necessary in this patient population, and by following these recommendations traumatic scenarios, prolonged drainage, extended hospitalizations, and/or surgery might be avoided in many cases.

chunks.title: Expert Statement: Pneumothorax Associated with Endoscopic Valve Therapy for Emphysema - Potential Mechanisms, Treatment Algorithm, and Case Examples
chunks.content: Pneumothorax rates after EBV vary by patient selection and degree of lobar exclusion. In early randomized cohorts with frequent incomplete occlusion, 90-day pneumothorax rates were approximately 4-5%. In case series achieving complete lobar exclusion, rates up to 29% were observed, and in current clinical practice with selection for absent collateral ventilation, rates up to 30% are reported. Pneumothorax typically occurs within 90 days of valve insertion; the median onset is 2 days and median duration is 11.5 days. Most cases resolve with observation or chest tube drainage. Patients experiencing pneumothorax often demonstrate substantial target lobar volume reduction, with reported mean reductions around 65%.

chunks.title: Bronchial Rheoplasty for Treatment of Chronic Bronchitis: Twelve-Month Results from a Multicenter Clinical Trial
chunks.content: Rationale: Chronic bronchitis (CB) is characterized by productive cough with excessive mucus production, resulting in quality-of-life impairment and increased exacerbation risk. Bronchial rheoplasty uses an endobronchial catheter to apply nonthermal pulsed electrical fields to the airways. Preclinical studies have demonstrated epithelial ablation followed by regeneration of normalized epithelium. Objectives: To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and initial outcomes of bronchial rheoplasty in patients with CB. Methods: Pooled analysis of two separate studies enrolling 30 patients undergoing bilateral bronchial rheoplasty was conducted. Follow-up through 6 months (primary outcome) and 12 months included assessment of adverse events, airway histology, and changes in symptoms using the Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) Assessment Test and St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ). Measurements and Main Results: Bronchial rheoplasty was performed in all 30 patients (63% male; mean [SD] age, 67 [7.4]; mean [SD] postbronchodilator FEV1, 65% [21%]; mean [SD] COPD Assessment Test score 25.6 [7.1]; mean [SD] SGRQ score, 59.6 [15.3]). There were no device-related and four procedure-related serious adverse events through 6 months, and there were none thereafter through 12 months. The most frequent nonserious, device- and/or procedure-related event through 6 months was mild hemoptysis in 47% (14 of 30) patients. Histologically, the mean goblet cell hyperplasia score was reduced by a statistically significant amount (P < 0.001). Significant changes from baseline to 6 months in COPD Assessment Test (mean, -7.9; median, -8.0; P = 0.0002) and SGRQ (mean, -14.6; median, -7.2; P = 0.0002) scores were observed, with similar observations through 12 months. Conclusions: This study provides the first clinical evidence of the feasibility, safety, and initial outcomes of bronchial rheoplasty in symptomatic patients with CB. Clinical trial registered with www.anzctr.org.au (AC

chunks.title: Bronchial Rheoplasty for Treatment of Chronic Bronchitis: Twelve-Month Results from a Multicenter Clinical Trial
chunks.content: Thirty patients were enrolled and completed bilateral bronchial rheoplasty (60 procedures). Mean (SD) age was 67 (7.4) years; 63.3% were male. Baseline mean (SD) post-bronchodilator FEV1% predicted was 65.0 (21.2); baseline CAT and SGRQ total scores were 25.6 (7.1) and 59.6 (15.3), respectively. A mean (SD) of 43 (21) activations were applied per lung; median hospital stay was 1 day (range 0-4), with 92% discharged within 48 hours. Through 6 months, there were no device-related SAEs and four procedure-related SAEs: pneumonia 2 days post-procedure (1), mucosal scarring related to cryobiopsy observed at second bronchoscopy (1), COPD exacerbation starting the day of the second procedure (1), and COPD exacerbation the day of the third bronchoscopy (1). No additional device- or procedure-related SAEs occurred from 6 to 12 months. The most frequent nonserious device/procedure-related AE through 6 months was mild hemoptysis in 14 of 30 patients (46.7%). Histology showed a statistically significant reduction in mean goblet cell hyperplasia score (P < 0.001). PROs improved from baseline to 6 months: CAT mean change -7.9 (median -8.0; P = 0.0002) and SGRQ mean change -14.6 (median -7.2; P = 0.0002), with similar observations through 12 months. Follow-up was available for 30/30 at 6 months and 29/30 at 12 months.

chunks.title: Two-Year Outcomes for the Double-Blind, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Study of Targeted Lung Denervation in Patients with Moderate to Severe COPD: AIRFLOW-2
chunks.content: Purpose: COPD exacerbations are associated with worsening clinical outcomes and increased healthcare costs, despite use of optimal medical therapy. A novel bronchoscopic therapy, targeted lung denervation (TLD), which disrupts parasympathetic pulmonary innervation of the lung, has been developed to reduce clinical consequences of cholinergic hyperactivity and its impact on COPD exacerbations. The AIRFLOW-2 study assessed the durability of safety and efficacy of TLD additive to optimal drug therapy compared to sham bronchoscopy and optimal drug therapy alone in subjects with moderate-to-severe, symptomatic COPD two years post randomization. Patients and Methods: TLD was performed in COPD patients (FEV1 30-60% predicted, CAT≥10 or mMRC≥2) in a 1:1 randomized, sham-controlled, double-blinded multicenter study (AIRFLOW-2) using a novel lung denervation system (Nuvaira, Inc., USA). Subjects remained blinded until their 12.5-month follow-up visit when control subjects were offered the opportunity to undergo TLD. A time-to-first-event analysis on moderate and severe and severe exacerbations of COPD was performed. Results: Eighty-two subjects (FEV1 41.6±7.4% predicted, 50.0% male, age 63.7±6.8 yrs, 24% with prior year respiratory hospitalization) were randomized. Time-to-first severe COPD exacerbation was significantly lengthened in the TLD arm (p=0.04, HR=0.38) at 2 years post-TLD therapy and trended towards similar attenuation for moderate and severe COPD exacerbations (p=0.18, HR=0.71). No significant changes in lung function or SGRQ-C were found 2 years post randomization between groups. Conclusion: In a randomized trial, TLD demonstrated a durable effect of significantly lower risk of severe AECOPD over 2 years. Further, lung function and quality of life remained stable following TLD. Clinical Trial Registration: NCT02058459.

chunks.title: Two-Year Outcomes for the Double-Blind, Randomized, Sham-Controlled Study of Targeted Lung Denervation in Patients with Moderate to Severe COPD: AIRFLOW-2
chunks.content: N=82 randomized (41 TLD, 41 control). At 2 years, retained: TLD n=36 (88%), control n=14 (after cross-over of 20 control subjects and 5 exits). Time-to-first severe COPD exacerbation requiring hospitalization was significantly lower with TLD vs control at 2 years (HR=0.38; 95% CI 0.15-0.99; p=0.04). No significant difference in time-to-first moderate or severe COPD exacerbation (HR=0.71; 95% CI 0.42-1.18; p=0.18). Annualized rate of moderate/severe exacerbations: control 0.81 vs TLD 0.64 (p=0.54). Annualized rate of severe exacerbations: control 0.15 vs TLD 0.11 (p=0.71). In year 2, respiratory-related hospitalization occurred in 11.1% of TLD subjects (4/36) vs 28.6% of control subjects (4/14). Lung function (FEV1, FVC, TLC, RV) and SGRQ-C remained stable with no significant between-group differences at 2 years.

chunks.title: Value of Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Percutaneous Gastrostomy: A Double-Blind Randomized Trial
chunks.content: Purpose: To compare peristomal infection rates following percutaneous gastrostomy (PG) after a single dose of prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo and evaluate rates of peristomal infection in patients receiving concurrent antibiotics. Materials and Methods: This single-center, randomized trial (2012-2016) enrolled 122 patients referred for image-guided PG; all enrolled patients completed the study. Of enrolled patients, 68 were randomly assigned to receive either antibiotics (n = 34) or placebo (n = 34) before PG placement. The remaining 54 patients were taking pre-existing antibiotics and were assigned to an observation arm. Stoma sites were assessed for signs of infection by a blinded evaluator at early (between 3-5 d and 7-10 d) and late (between 14-17 d and 28-30 d) time points after the procedure. The primary outcome was peristomal infection. Results: Under intention-to-treat analysis, early infection rate was 11.8% (4/34 patients; 95% CI, 0.0%-9.4%) in the placebo arm and 0.0% (0/34 patients; 95% CI, 0.0%-8.4%) in the antibiotic arm (P = .057 for comparison of infections in the 2 arms). Under per-protocol analysis, early infection rate was 13.3% (4/30 patients; 95% CI, 4.4%-29.1%) in the placebo arm and 0.0% (0/32 patients; 95% CI, 0.0%-8.9%) in the antibiotic arm (P = .049). The number needed to treat to prevent 1 early infection was 8.5 and 7.5 from the 2 analyses, respectively. Conclusions: There is a trend toward reduction in rate of peristomal infection after PG when prophylactic antibiotics are administered.

chunks.title: Value-Based Proposition for a Dedicated Interventional Pulmonology Suite: An Adaptable Business Model
chunks.content: Value-based care is evolving with a focus on improving efficiency, reducing cost, and enhancing the patient experience. Interventional pulmonology has the opportunity to lead an effective value-based care model. This model is supported by the relatively low cost of pulmonary procedures and has the potential to improve efficiencies in thoracic care. We discuss key strategies to evaluate and improve efficiency in interventional pulmonology practice and describe our experience in developing an interventional pulmonology suite. Such a model can be adapted to other specialty areas and may encourage a more coordinated approach to specialty care.

chunks.source_file: Value-Based Proposition for a Dedicated IP suite.oe_final.json
chunks.title: Value-Based Proposition for a Dedicated Interventional Pulmonology Suite: An Adaptable Business Model
chunks.content: Process mapping identified opportunities to improve efficiency via standardized orders, documentation templates, and streamlined changeover procedures. IP procedures were decentralized across multiple hospital locations (ultrasound department, ambulatory surgery unit, endoscopy unit, and OR). The team proposed consolidating procedures into a dedicated IP suite to improve access, throughput, and cost-effectiveness, while enabling high-risk procedures to be performed safely with specialized staff. Market and SWOT analyses supported the business case, highlighting competitive differentiation, potential to reduce outmigration, and downstream revenue growth through enhanced cancer care pathways.

chunks.title: Variable Learning Curve of Basic Rigid Bronchoscopy in Trainees
chunks.content: Background: Despite increased use of rigid bronchoscopy (RB) for therapeutic indications and recommendations from professional societies to use performance-based competency, an assessment tool has not been utilized to measure the competency of trainees to perform RB in clinical settings. Objectives: The aim of the study was to evaluate a previously developed assessment tool - Rigid Bronchoscopy Tool for Assessment of Skills and Competence (RIGID-TASC) - for determining the RB learning curve of interventional pulmonary (IP) trainees in the clinical setting and explore the variability of learning curve of trainees. Methods: IP fellows at 4 institutions were enrolled. After preclinical simulation training, all RBs performed in patients were scored by faculty using RIGID-TASC until competency threshold was achieved. Competency threshold was defined as unassisted RB intubation and navigation through the central airways on 3 consecutive patients at the first attempt with a minimum score of 89. A regression-based model was devised to construct and compare the learning curves. Results: Twelve IP fellows performed 178 RBs. Trainees reached the competency threshold between 5 and 24 RBs, with a median of 15 RBs (95% CI, 6-21). There were differences among trainees in learning curve parameters including starting point, slope, and inflection point, as demonstrated by the curve-fitting model. Subtasks that required the highest number of procedures (median = 10) to gain competency included ability to intubate at the first attempt and intubation time of <60 s. Conclusions: Trainees acquire RB skills at a variable pace, and RIGID-TASC can be used to assess learning curve of IP trainees in clinical settings.

chunks.title: Variable Learning Curve of Basic Rigid Bronchoscopy in Trainees
chunks.content: Twelve participants contributed 178 RB procedures. Indications were malignant central airway obstruction (38%), nonmalignant central airway obstruction (53%), and other (9%). Trainees achieved the competency threshold (3 consecutive scores ≥89 on first attempt) between 5 and 24 RB procedures (median 15; 95% CI, 6-21). Cumulative incidence showed 25% competent at 9 procedures (95% CI, 5-15), 50% at 15 (95% CI, 6-21), 75% at 20 (95% CI, 15-24), and 100% at 24. Learning curves varied across trainees in starting point, slope, and inflection point. Subtasks requiring the most attempts to reach subtask competency included first-attempt intubation (median 10, IQR 8-16) and completing intubation within 60 s (median 9.5, IQR 7-18.2). Reported complications across all procedures included 1 loose tooth, 2 upper airway mucosal injuries, 2 lower airway mucosal injuries, and 2 hypoxemia events with oxygen saturation ≤88%.

chunks.title: Ambulatory management of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax: a randomised controlled trial
chunks.content: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) is traditionally managed with an intercostal chest tube attached to an underwater seal. We investigated whether use of a one-way flutter valve shortened patients’ length of stay (LoS). This open-label randomised controlled trial enrolled patients presenting with SSP and randomised to either a chest tube and underwater seal (standard care: SC) or ambulatory care (AC) with a flutter valve. The type of flutter valve used depended on whether at randomisation the patient already had a chest tube in place: in those without a chest tube a pleural vent (PV) was used; in those with a chest tube in situ, an Atrium Pneumostat (AP) valve was attached. The primary end-point was LoS. Between March 2017 and March 2020, 41 patients underwent randomisation: 20 to SC and 21 to AC (13=PV, 8=AP). There was no difference in LoS in the first 30 days following treatment intervention: AC (median=6 days, IQR 14.5) and SC (median=6 days, IQR 13.3). In patients treated with PV there was a high rate of early treatment failure (6/13; 46%), compared to patients receiving SC (3/20; 15%) (p=0.11). Patients treated with AP had no (0/8; 0%) early treatment failures and a median LoS of 1.5 days (IQR 23.8). There was no difference in LoS between ambulatory and standard care. Pleural Vents had high rates of treatment failure and should not be used in SSP. Atrium Pneumostats are a safer alternative, with a trend towards lower LoS.

chunks.title: Ambulatory management of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax: a randomised controlled trial
chunks.content: Forty-one participants were randomised: 21 ambulatory (13 PV, 8 AP) and 20 standard care. Primary outcome: total hospitalisation in first 30 days median 6 days (IQR 1-15.5) ambulatory vs 6 days (IQR 2.25-15.5) standard care (p=0.77). Initial admission LoS: 1 day (IQR 1-14) ambulatory vs 3.5 days (IQR 2-7) standard (p=0.122). Time until medically fit for discharge: 1 day (IQR 1-1) ambulatory vs 2 days (IQR 2-6) standard (p=0.001). Time to chest tube removal: 3 days (IQR 1.5-9) ambulatory vs 2 days (IQR 1-6) standard (p=0.36). Failure of initial treatment within first week: 6/21 (28%) ambulatory vs 3/20 (15%) standard (p=0.29). Additional pleural procedure within 3 months: 8/21 (38%) ambulatory vs 6/20 (30%) standard (p=0.59). Thoracic surgery: 6/21 (29%) ambulatory vs 6/20 (30%) standard. Medical pleurodesis: 2/21 (10%) vs 2/20 (10%). Six-month ipsilateral recurrence: 4/21 (19%) vs 4/20 (20%). Subgroup within ambulatory: early treatment failure 0/8 (0%) AP vs 6/13 (46%) PV (p=0.046). An urgent safety review halted PV use due to high early failure.

chunks.source_file: What is the value of electromagnetic navigation in lung cancer and to what extent does it require improvement .oe_final.json
chunks.title: What is the value of electromagnetic navigation in lung cancer and to what extent does it require improvement?
chunks.content: Introduction: Lung nodules are being identified with increasing frequency. With this growing burden of nodules comes a growing need for diagnostic technologies extending beyond the current reach of conventional bronchoscopy. One such method for diagnosing peripheral lung lesions is electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy (ENB), which comprises a set of tools designed to aid the bronchoscopist in identifying, accessing, and sampling peripheral lung lesions under virtual guidance. Areas covered: Herein we present an in-depth review of ENB, including commercially available electromagnetic navigation platforms, factors influencing diagnostic yield, adjunctive imaging and biopsy tools, potential risks, cost, technical shortcomings, and competing technologies. A review of the scientific literature was conducted primarily through PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, and pertinent publications and abstracts from the inception of electromagnetic navigation through early 2020 were considered. We also share our perspective on the future of ENB from both a diagnostic and a therapeutic standpoint. Expert opinion: ENB is currently a leading tool in the diagnostic evaluation of peripheral lung lesions. The future of ENB rests not only on its potential to expand into the therapeutic realm but also on its ability to keep pace with competing diagnostic and therapeutic technologies.

chunks.title: What is the value of electromagnetic navigation in lung cancer and to what extent does it require improvement?
chunks.content: The review describes three FDA-approved electromagnetic navigation platforms (superDimension, Veran SPiN, and Auris Monarch), outlines ENB workflow (planning, registration, navigation), factors influencing diagnostic yield (lesion size, location, bronchus sign, and biopsy modality), adjunctive tools (radial EBUS, fluoroscopy, cone-beam CT), risks (pneumothorax, bleeding, respiratory failure), and key limitations such as CT-to-body divergence. Reported diagnostic yield in the literature varies, with the largest recent prospective study cited at 73%. The authors discuss future directions including mitigation of CT-to-body divergence, integration with advanced imaging and fluoroscopic navigation, and potential therapeutic applications.

chunks.title: Microwave ablation via a flexible catheter for the treatment of nonsurgical peripheral lung cancer: A pilot study
chunks.content: Background: Endobronchial microwave ablation via flexible catheter offers the potential for local therapy for inoperable peripheral lung cancer. The study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of navigation bronchoscopy-guided water-cooled microwave ablation catheter for nonsurgical peripheral lung cancer. Methods: This was a prospective single arm pilot study. Patients with early stage or multiple primary peripheral lung cancer who were nonsurgical candidates for surgery were enrolled in the study. Bronchoscopic microwave ablation was performed via a flexible water-cooled microwave ablation antenna under the guidance of navigation bronchoscopy. Radial probe endobronchial ultrasound combined with fluoroscopy was used to confirm the position. Treatment outcomes were evaluated based on follow-up chest CT and positron emission tomography scans. Primary endpoints were technical success and safety. Secondary endpoints were complete ablation rate, 2-year local control rate, and progression-free survival. Results: Thirteen patients were enrolled in the study from April 2018 to July 2019. A total of 19 sessions of microwave ablation were performed on 14 tumors under the guidance of navigation bronchoscopy. The technical success was 100%. Treatment-related complications occurred in two patients. The complete ablation rate was 78.6% (11/14). The 2-year local control rate was 71.4%. Median progression-free survival was 33 months for all patients. Conclusions: In this pilot study, bronchoscopic microwave ablation appears to be feasible with acceptable occurrence of complication in the treatment of peripheral lung cancer under the guidance of navigation bronchoscopy.

chunks.title: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy versus percutaneous radiological gastrostomy for swallowing disturbances
chunks.content: Background: Gastrostomy is standard for long-term enteral nutrition in individuals with swallowing disturbances. Percutaneous gastrostomy can be performed via endoscopy (PEG) or radiological guidance (PRG), each with different limitations, advantages, and contraindications. Numerous studies have compared these techniques, but the optimal method regarding efficacy and safety remains unclear. Objectives: To compare the safety and efficacy of PEG and PRG in individuals with swallowing disturbances. Search methods: CENTRAL (January 2016), MEDLINE (1946 to 22 January 2016), EMBASE (1980 to 22 January 2016), reference lists, ongoing trial databases including the Chinese Cochrane Centre Controlled Trials Register, and PubMed; no language restrictions. Selection criteria: RCTs comparing PEG with PRG in individuals with swallowing disturbances. Data collection and analysis: Two authors independently screened and assessed study quality; no meta-analysis due to absence of eligible RCTs. Main results: No RCTs were identified. Observational evidence suggests both PEG and PRG can be safely performed in selected individuals, with both major and minor complications reported. A definitive RCT is needed to determine the preferred technique. Authors’ conclusions: PEG and PRG are both effective for long-term enteral nutrition in selected individuals; current evidence is insufficient to recommend one over the other. Technique choice should be based on indications/contraindications, operator experience, and available facilities. Large-scale RCTs are required.

chunks.title: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy versus percutaneous radiological gastrostomy for swallowing disturbances
chunks.content: No randomized controlled trials comparing PEG vs PRG for swallowing disturbances were identified. Existing evidence comprises retrospective, non-randomized studies and case series, indicating both techniques are feasible and generally safe in selected populations, with reported major and minor complications. No direct randomized evidence enables comparative estimates of efficacy or safety between PEG and PRG.

chunks.title: Whole Lung Lavage Treatment of Chinese Patients with Autoimmune Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis: A Retrospective Long‑term Follow‑up Study
chunks.content: Background: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is a rare lung disease, the most common type of which is autoimmune PAP. The gold standard therapy for PAP is whole lung lavage (WLL). Few studies have reported the optimal technique with which to evaluate the response to WLL. In this study, we aimed to identify parameters with which to assess the need for repeat WLL during a long‑term 8‑year follow‑up. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of 120 patients with autoimmune PAP with 80 of whom underwent WLL. Physiologic, serologic, and radiologic features of the patients were analyzed during an 8‑year follow‑up after the first WLL treatment. Results: Of the 40 patients without any intervention, 39 patients either achieved remission or remained stable and only one died of pulmonary infection. Of the 56 patients who underwent WLL for 1 time, 55 remained free from a second WLL and 1 patient died of cancer. Twenty‑four required additional treatments after their first WLL. The baseline PaO2 (P = 0.000), PA‑aO2 (P = 0.000), shunt fraction rate (P = 0.001), percent of predicted normal diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO%Pred) (P = 0.016), 6‑min walk test (P = 0.013), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (P = 0.007), and neuron‑specific enolase (NSE) (P = 0.003) showed significant differences among the three groups. The need for a second WLL was significantly associated with PaO2 (P = 0.000), CEA (P = 0.050), the 6‑minute walk test (P = 0.026), and DLCO%Pred (P = 0.041). The DLCO%Pred on admission with a cut‑off value of 42.1% (P = 0.001) may help to distinguish whether patients with PAP require a second WLL. Conclusions: WLL is the optimal treatment method for PAP and provides remarkable improvements for affected patients. The DLCO%Pred on admission with a cut‑off value of 42.1% may distinguish whether patients with PAP require a second WLL.

In the single‑WLL group, 55/56 remained free from second WLL; 1 died of lung cancer ~3 years post‑diagnosis. Of the multiple‑WLL group (n=24), 13 were stable, 6 in remission, and 5 progressed at follow‑up end. Baseline comparisons across WLL‑times groups showed significant differences in PaO2 (P = 0.000), PA‑aO2 (P = 0.000), shunt fraction (P = 0.001), DLCO%Pred (P = 0.016), 6‑min walk test (P = 0.013), CEA (P = 0.007), and NSE (P = 0.003). chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Transparenchymal Nodule Access
chunks.content: BTPNA creates a planned transparenchymal tunnel from an airway point-of-entry (POE) to a peripheral pulmonary nodule. High diagnostic yield (≈73–75 %) including nodules without a bronchus sign. Lower pneumothorax risk than TTNA by using an avascular, airway-based pathway. Requires advanced navigation (Archimedes VBN) and fused fluoroscopy under general anesthesia. Working channel requirements: ≥2.0 mm for Fle XNeedle+balloon; ≥2.8 mm when using a sheath.

chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Transparenchymal Nodule Access
chunks.content: BTPNA Planning: Obtain high-resolution chest CT and reconstruct 3D model with navigation software (e.g., Archimedes). Identify an optimal POE on the airway wall and an avascular path to the nodule. Confirm feasibility relative to nearby critical structures on CT (vessels, heart, esophagus).

chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Transparenchymal Nodule Access
chunks.content: Navigation and pathway setup: Insert bronchoscope and navigate to the predetermined POE under navigation guidance. Puncture the airway wall with a coring needle or Fle XNeedle to create the initial opening. Dilate the puncture with a balloon catheter to establish a tunnel entrance. Advance a sheath with a blunt dissection stylet through lung parenchyma to the lesion under real-time fluoroscopy/navigation.

chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Transparenchymal Nodule Access
chunks.content: Sampling through sheath: Remove the blunt stylet and use forceps, brush, and/or needle aspiration through the sheath to obtain tissue. Employ multiple sampling tools to maximize representativeness.

chunks.title: Cricothyroidotomy
chunks.content: Cricothyroidotomy is the quickest route to stabilize the airway when intubation fails. Surgical airway is the endpoint of difficult airway algorithms. In children <10–12 years, needle cricothyroidotomy is preferred; convert to tracheostomy as soon as feasible.

chunks.title: Cricothyroidotomy
chunks.content: Needle cricothyroidotomy (temporizing, adults): Identify CT membrane via midline palpation; alternative: 3–4 fingerbreadths above suprasternal notch with neck neutral. Use large-bore catheter-over-needle (e.g., 14-g) attached to syringe partially filled with saline/water. Advance at ~45° angle caudally through skin and CT membrane while aspirating; air bubbles confirm entry. Withdraw needle, leave cannula; connect oxygen tubing. Deliver oxygen at 10–12 L/min; use Y-connector to allow periodic CO₂ release.

chunks.title: Cricothyroidotomy
chunks.content: Open surgical cricothyroidotomy (standard): Prep anterior neck from mandible angle to sternal notch; maintain sterile technique; position with mandible anteriorly displaced. Stabilize larynx with thumb and long finger; use index finger to palpate and reidentify CT membrane throughout. Make a 2 cm midline vertical skin incision over CT membrane, staying strictly in midline to avoid anterior jugular veins. Palpate CT membrane through incision and make a horizontal incision in the lower half of the membrane. Insert cricoid hook and apply gentle upward traction on cricoid; avoid traction on thyroid to protect vocal folds.

chunks.title: Cricothyroidotomy
chunks.content: Rapid 4‑Step Technique (RFST): Operator at head of bed; identify landmarks and stabilize. Horizontal stab incision through skin, subcutaneous tissue, and CT membrane to access airway. Stabilize larynx by hooking cricoid cartilage; apply upward traction. Insert tracheostomy tube as per standard technique and confirm placement.

chunks.title: Electrocautery and Argon Plasma Coagulation
chunks.content: Needle knife radial incisions for webs/stenosis: Position needle-knife at 12 o'clock; short activation to incise superficially. Repeat at 3 and 9 o'clock (and additional quadrants if needed). Avoid posterior membranous wall to prevent esophageal injury. Follow with CRE balloon dilation until adequate lumen achieved.

metadata.procedure_name: Needle knife radial incisions for webs/stenosis

chunks.title: Electrocautery and Argon Plasma Coagulation
chunks.content: Snare excision for pedunculated tumors: Loop snare at stalk base; tighten to compress blood supply. Apply EC in brief bursts while tightening until release. Retrieve specimen with forceps; treat base for hemostasis.

chunks.title: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy
chunks.content: Targeted lung denervation (TLD) ablates parasympathetic vagal fibers with radiofrequency to reduce bronchoconstriction and exacerbations in COPD. Bronchial rheoplasty applies non-thermal pulsed electrical energy to ablate goblet cells and reduce sputum burden in chronic bronchitis. Spray cryotherapy delivers metered liquid nitrogen at approximately −196 °C to ablate abnormal mucosa and reduce mucus hypersecretion. Careful phenotype-based selection is essential: TLD for frequent exacerbators; rheoplasty and spray cryotherapy for chronic bronchitis with high symptom burden. Preprocedure CT is required for TLD to assess bronchial anatomy and exclude severe emphysema (emphysema index >50% at −950 HU).

chunks.title: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy
chunks.content: Targeted Lung Denervation (TLD): General anesthesia; insert dual-cooled radiofrequency catheter via bronchoscope. Position catheter circumferentially in each main bronchus to ablate vagal fibers at four positions. Use esophageal balloon with contrast to maintain distance from esophagus and avoid gastric vagal ablation. Energy selection based on anatomy (26–32 W); radiofrequency activation for 120 s followed by 30 s postcooling. Administer prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids; typical total procedure time ≈74 min.

chunks.title: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy
chunks.content: Bronchial Rheoplasty: Under general anesthesia, perform two sessions: right lung then 4–6 weeks later left lung. Reduce FiO2 to 30% during activations. Deploy catheter in subsegmental bronchi and advance proximally toward main carina, treating each segment. Expand electrode to contact mucosa; apply current for 5 s per activation; collapse and move to next site. Typical duration ≈40 min with ~40–60 activations per side; administer corticosteroids to reduce COPD exacerbation risk.

chunks.title: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy
chunks.content: Spray Cryotherapy (Metered Cryospray): Insert delivery catheter through bronchoscope; connect to liquid-nitrogen console. Deliver liquid nitrogen as radial spray with thermocouple feedback to create an ≈10 mm circular ablation zone (depth 0.1–0.5 mm). Stop ventilation during application and usually deflate endotracheal tube cuff to avoid barotrauma or asphyxia. Perform three procedures: (1) right lower lobe + right mainstem, (2) left lower lobe + left mainstem, (3) both upper lobes + distal trachea; do not treat right middle lobe. Mean number of sprays ≈20 per procedure; mean procedure time ≈34 min.

chunks.title: Endobronchial Silicone Stents for Airway Management
chunks.content: Silicone stent deployment (rigid bronchoscopy): Induce general anesthesia; perform rigid bronchoscopy. Pre‑treat: mechanical tumor debulking and/or airway dilation as needed. Measure lesion length endoscopically; confirm CT‑based estimate; select a stent extending 5 mm beyond lesion proximally and distally. Select diameter based on maximal dilation caliber (trachea 14–16 mm; mainstem 12–13 mm; BI 10–11 mm). Load stent into introducer; position just distal to lesion; pull back to final position with rigid forceps.

chunks.title: Endobronchial Silicone Stents for Airway Management
chunks.content: Temporary stent trial for suspected malacia: Place temporary stent as internal splinting. If clinical improvement: refer for external stenting; consider stent removal. If no improvement: remove stent; recommend physiotherapy and CPAP.

chunks.source_file: Interventional Pulmonary and Advanced Bronchoscopy Training.json
chunks.title: Interventional Pulmonary and Advanced Bronchoscopy Training
chunks.content: IP training has evolved from apprenticeship to structured fellowships with certification. Simulation plays a critical role in competency development but lacks standardized adoption. Procedural volume requirements differ between US (higher) and Europe (lower). Validated assessment tools exist (RIGID-TASC, EBUS-STAT, CAPS, TUBE-iCOMPT) but are underutilized. CME is vital as new technologies outpace traditional fellowship curricula.

chunks.title: Large Bore Chest Tubes
chunks.content: Large-bore chest tubes are generally defined as ≥20 F; inner diameter varies by material/manufacturer. Clinical indications persist for high-PEEP ventilated pneumothorax, BPF, emergencies/trauma, select hemothorax, and postthoracic surgery pneumothorax. Surgical/blunt dissection via the mid-axillary 'safe triangle' is the preferred technique; trocar insertion is discouraged. Three-bottle drainage systems (trap, water seal, manometer) underpin modern commercial drains; dry suction variants exist. Small-bore tubes (<20 F) are often as effective as large-bore but with lower pain scores; choose size based on scenario rather than dogma.

chunks.title: Large Bore Chest Tubes
chunks.content: Large-bore chest tube insertion – surgical/blunt dissection: Position patient supine or ~45° with ipsilateral arm abducted and externally rotated. Identify the safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, and a line superior to the nipple/submammary fold. Prep and drape; infiltrate ~20 m L lidocaine to dermis, subcutaneous tissues, intercostal space/periosteum, and parietal pleura. Aspirate air or fluid during anesthetic to confirm pleural entry; if none, reconfirm with ultrasound. Make ~2 cm incision over the rib; bluntly dissect through serratus/intercostal muscles along the superior rib border.

metadata.procedure_name: Large-bore chest tube insertion – surgical/blunt dissection

chunks.title: Large Bore Chest Tubes
chunks.content: Seldinger technique for large-bore tubes (less common): Over-the-wire placement with serial dilation (up to three dilators may be required for catheters up to 32 F). Lacks digital palpation and manual guidance advantages of the blunt dissection technique.

metadata.procedure_name: Seldinger technique for large-bore tubes (less common)

chunks.title: Large Bore Chest Tubes
chunks.content: Postprocedure management and removal: Select analgesia with NSAIDs and/or opioids; NSAIDs do not impair pleurodesis at 3 months in malignant effusion. Consider clamping trials for pneumothorax, noting ACCP expert split; digital air-leak devices can hasten removal if no leak is measured. Outpatient Heimlich valve is reasonable for persistent air leak on water seal when criteria are met (asymptomatic, no subcutaneous emphysema after 14 days, stable pleural space). For pleural effusion, reported removal thresholds vary widely (<100 to <500 m L/24 h); after lung resection, <5 m L/kg/24 h vs <200 m L/24 h show similar outcomes. Remove the tube rapidly during positive intrathoracic pressure (patient humming) or during an inspiratory hold on the ventilator.

chunks.title: Malignant Central Airway Obstruction
chunks.content: MCAO is defined as ≥50% narrowing of a central airway (trachea, mainstem bronchi, bronchus intermedius, or lobar bronchi) by malignancy. Therapeutic bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is the backbone of multimodality management and bridges to definitive oncologic therapy. Classifying obstruction as intrinsic, extrinsic, or mixed guides modality selection and prognosis. Airway stents palliate extrinsic compression and maintain patency after debridement but require careful follow-up and removal once tumor regresses. For immediate-effect ablation, reduce FiO2 to ≤0.4 and keep probe tips away from flammable devices to decrease airway fire risk.

chunks.title: Malignant Central Airway Obstruction
chunks.content: Therapeutic bronchoscopy planning and anesthesia: Perform comprehensive airway-focused preassessment (mouth opening >3 finger breadths, teeth status, modified Mallampati, neck mobility >90°, thyromental distance >3 finger breadths). Plan anesthesia with general anesthesia/deep sedation and paralytics for therapeutic bronchoscopy; coordinate with anesthesiology. Select ventilatory support (jet ventilation or controlled/spontaneous assisted ventilation) based on local expertise and patient status; consider ECMO standby for critical obstructions.

chunks.title: Malignant Central Airway Obstruction
chunks.content: Tumor debridement and immediate-effect ablation: Debulk endobronchial tumor using rigid or flexible forceps; consider rigid bronchoscope bevel for coring proximal tumors. Apply immediate-effect ablative modalities (electrocautery probes, snare/knife; APC; laser) to achieve hemostasis and vaporize tumor. Maintain FiO2 ≤0.4 and keep active probe tip away from flammable devices to reduce airway fire risk.

chunks.title: Malignant Central Airway Obstruction
chunks.content: Delayed-effect local therapies: Consider photodynamic therapy (PDT) to reduce tumor regrowth in appropriate candidates. Recognize that brachytherapy and cryotherapy have limited current utilization in many centers.

chunks.title: General Principles of Mediastinal Cryobiopsy
chunks.content: EBUS-TBNA is guideline-recommended as the initial approach for mediastinal staging in lung cancer. EBUS-TBMCB provides larger, intact samples and can improve diagnostic yield, particularly for benign and uncommon entities; safety is generally acceptable. A combined approach (EBUS-TBNA + cryobiopsy) can enhance adequacy for molecular/immunologic testing without increasing complications. Transesophageal mediastinal cryobiopsy is an alternative route when tracheal access is not feasible.

chunks.title: General Principles of Mediastinal Cryobiopsy
chunks.content: Indications and contraindications for EBUS-TBMCB: Indications: at least one mediastinal lesion with short-axis ≥1 cm on thoracic imaging; newly discovered mediastinal lesions; clinical symptoms needing biopsy to establish etiology. Contraindications: severe cardiopulmonary disease, coagulation disorders, intolerance to anesthesia or endoscopic procedures, psychiatric disorders, severe neurosis.

chunks.title: General Principles of Mediastinal Cryobiopsy
chunks.content: Anesthesia for EBUS-TBMCB: Supine position; upper airway topical anesthesia with 2% lidocaine. Conscious sedation with IV midazolam and fentanyl. Administer oxygen 1–2 L/min; increase if SpO2 <90%. Continuous monitoring of vital signs and pulse oximetry.

chunks.title: General Principles of Mediastinal Cryobiopsy
chunks.content: Systematic EBUS examination: Insert EBUS bronchoscope via nasal route (oral route if nasal passage unsuitable). Sequentially examine mediastinal and hilar stations per Mountain-Dressler map. Use Doppler to assess blood supply; measure long and short axes. Select the most suspicious lesion with relatively lower biopsy risk as target.

chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Management of Persistent Air Leaks
chunks.content: Endobronchial one‑way valve placement (EBV/SVS): Size airway using deployment system; choose valve size. Place valve(s) to occlude all contributing segments. Confirm air leak reduction at chest drainage device; adjust as needed.

chunks.title: Bronchoscopic Management of Persistent Air Leaks
chunks.content: Watanabe spigot (EWS) bronchial occlusion: Select spigot size; advance to target segment. Wedge and seat securely; reassess air leak. Combine with chemical pleurodesis when appropriate.

chunks.title: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Approach to Pneumothorax
chunks.content: Pneumothorax is classified as primary/secondary spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic; severity is determined by size, symptoms, and physiologic compromise. POCUS is highly sensitive and specific for pneumothorax and should be prioritized when available; chest radiography and CT remain complementary. Management is increasingly individualized: many stable, minimally symptomatic PSPs can be managed conservatively with robust follow‑up. When intervention is required, needle aspiration and small‑bore tube thoracostomy are effective; ambulatory options can reduce length of stay. Persistent air leak (PAL) requires a multidisciplinary strategy ranging from chemical/mechanical pleurodesis and VATS to autologous blood patch and endobronchial valves. Tension pneumothorax is a life‑threatening emergency requiring immediate decompression followed by tube thoracostomy.

chunks.title: Physiology of Fixed Airway Obstruction
chunks.content: Upper airway obstruction frequently presents to the interventional bronchoscopist with causes including malignant tracheal disease and postintubation stenosis. Physiological changes are due to turbulent airflow at stenosis, leading to increased resistance, higher work of breathing, hypoventilation, and exercise limitation. Characteristic changes are seen on pulmonary function tests, especially flow-volume loops. Fixed obstruction shows plateauing of inspiratory and expiratory limbs, differentiating it from variable intrathoracic or extrathoracic obstruction. Spirometry and quantitative indices (e.g., FEV1/PEFR ≥ 10, FEV1/FEV0.5 ≥ 1.5) are useful but lack sensitivity; bronchoscopy and imaging are essential.

chunks.title: Quality Indicators and Performance Monitoring in Interventional Pulmonology
chunks.content: Performance monitoring systematically collects and analyzes metrics to improve bronchoscopy outcomes. Quality indicators are measurable elements of practice performance linked to patient safety and outcomes. Indicators fall into structural, process, and outcome measures. Audit and feedback are critical for reducing variance in care and improving quality. Large audits and registries (BTS, AQuIRE) have highlighted gaps in quality and informed performance standards.

chunks.title: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
chunks.content: Two‑slide pull smear technique: Expel aspirate onto slide A; use slide B to gently spread into two thin smears. Air‑dry one slide for Diff‑Quik/Giemsa; fix the other in ethanol for Papanicolaou.

chunks.title: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
chunks.content: ROSE adequacy workflow: Assess for lymphoid tissue or lesional cells; note artifacts (mucus, ciliated cells, cartilage). Communicate adequacy to bronchoscopist; adjust passes accordingly. Allocate additional material to cell block (FFPE) for ancillary testing.

chunks.title: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
chunks.content: Cell block preparation (FFPE): Rinse residual material with ~50% ethanol and centrifuge to pellet. Fix in formalin and embed in paraffin for IHC/FISH/NGS.

chunks.title: Single Use Bronchoscopes
chunks.content: Diagnostic uses: Airway inspection; photographic documentation. BAL and washings via working channel. Brushings and transbronchial biopsies per protocol.

chunks.title: Single Use Bronchoscopes
chunks.content: Therapeutic uses: Suction for mucus plugs, blood/clots. Support for tumor debulking (mechanical/energy adjuncts), stent deployment, foreign body removal. Guidance for percutaneous tracheostomy; BLVR tools; bronchial thermoplasty; fiducial placement.

chunks.title: Small-Bore Drain Types and Placement
chunks.content: Small-bore chest tubes (≤14 F) are effective for most pleural drainage indications with better tolerability than large-bore tubes. Ultrasound guidance is the modality of choice for site selection and has become the standard of care for SBCT placement. Common SBCT indications include pleural infection, malignant pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and selected hemothorax scenarios. Seldinger technique is the preferred insertion method; trocar insertion should generally be avoided due to organ injury risk. Routine suction is not recommended for pneumothorax management; water seal often suffices. Complication rates are low with image guidance and experienced operators; major complications are rare.

chunks.title: Thoracentesis Technique
chunks.content: Thoracentesis (diagnostic and therapeutic): Position patient sitting upright; consider lateral decubitus if unstable. Perform consent and time-out; mark correct side. Use ultrasound in real time to localize effusion and optimal intercostal space. Prep skin with chlorhexidine or betadine; place sterile drape; wear mask and sterile gloves. Anesthetize skin and intercostal tract with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine using 25-gauge then 22-gauge 2.5-in needle.

chunks.title: Transbronchial Cryobiopsy in Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disorders
chunks.content: TBLC is increasingly first-line when histopathology is needed for diffuse parenchymal lung disease. General anesthesia with airway control is common; bronchial blockers are strongly recommended to prevent/mitigate major bleeding. Common guiding systems include fluoroscopy; CBCT, CLE, radial EBUS, and OCT are useful in selected cases. Cryoprobes: 1.1 mm, 1.7 mm, 2.4 mm (length 1150 mm); typical freezing times: 2.4 mm ≈ 6 s; 1.7 mm ≈ 8 s; 1.1 mm ≈ 12–13 s. Diagnostic yield is ~80% with larger samples than forceps TBB; pneumothorax is the most frequent complication (mean ~5%; range <1–30%). Relative contraindications include FVC <50% predicted, DLCO <35% predicted, PAPs >40 mmHg, significant emphysema, and recent clinical deterioration; coagulopathy/instability are absolute.

chunks.title: Transthoracic Needle Biopsy
chunks.content: : Obtain helical CT to plan trajectory avoiding vessels, fissures, bullae Administer local anesthesia ± sedation (midazolam/fentanyl) Advance coaxial introducer needle under CT fluoroscopy Perform FNA and/or core biopsy (typically 2–5 passes, ≥4 cores for molecular testing) Seal tract with saline, hydrogel plug, or ABPI

chunks.title: Y-Stenting Techniques
chunks.content: Y-shaped airway stents treat central airway obstruction involving the lower trachea, main carina, and proximal mainstem bronchi. Main indications include malignant stenosis (often from adjacent lung cancer) and select benign conditions (e.g., post-tracheostomy stenosis, tracheobronchomalacia) when surgery is not feasible. Stent families: polymer (e.g., Dumon), hybrid (Dynamic), and self-expandable metallic; choice depends on airway biomechanics and lesion morphology. Rigid bronchoscopy is preferred; metallic Y-stents are commonly deployed over two guidewires under fluoroscopy. Frequent adverse events include mucostasis and granulation tissue; migration is uncommon with Y-stents due to their geometry. Comparative data suggest higher insertion success and shorter implantation time with metallic Y-stents versus silicone, with similar early/late complications.
